Benchmark and evaluate tool-using LLM agents on realistic, hard tasks against real-world MCP servers connected to actual data sources, not simplified or simulated environments, so evaluation reflects authentic operational complexity.
Minimize the exposed tool space to the tools relevant to the task: connecting additional unrelated MCP servers enlarges the tool space, injects noise, and measurably degrades agent success.

Evaluate MCP tool-use agents on large-scale, multi-server, dynamic toolsets that force real tool retrieval and multi-tool composition; do not rely on single-server setups that inject a fixed tool list directly into the model context.

Evaluate agent tool-use on three axes at once — realistic cross-server multi-step workflows, breadth across authentic (non-mock) servers, and reproducible claim-level scoring disentangled from verbosity and style; do not accept a benchmark that satisfies only one or two.

Recognize that on realistic multi-server tool-use tasks the agentic frontier is not saturated and is no longer explained by function-calling mechanics alone, so evaluations must probe evidence-gathering, stopping, and synthesis.

For coding agents, rely on deterministic outcome tests (does the code run, do the tests pass) plus an LLM rubric for overall code quality, adding heuristic code-quality rules and transcript grading of tool/user interaction only as needed.

Minimize the complexity of the parameters the LLM must construct for a tool call; an MCP's effectiveness rises as the LLM-built parameters are simplified or optimized, and falls when the hardest construction work is offloaded to the model.

Optimize MCP-agent efficiency by targeting protocol orchestration - schema injection, planning, transport, and result handling - not tool execution speed, which is a negligible cost fraction under lightweight-to-moderate tools.

Expect customized MCP clients to be input-bottlenecked: LLM planning plus tool-schema injection dominate their token and latency budgets, and cloud custom setups carry a planning/prefill latency floor that grows with task complexity.

Prioritize agent-memory and MCP-caching optimizations, because on the evaluated tool-heavy multi-turn workloads they cut end-to-end latency by up to 13x, input tokens by up to 88%, and cost by up to 66% while raising completion rates.

Design an MCP server for a large-API platform as a capability-oriented interface: expose a small set of generic verb tools and put the intelligence in a declarative registry that maps each resource type to its API operations, rather than wrapping one tool per endpoint. Adding a resource type then means adding one registry entry, keeping the LLM's tool vocabulary constant and letting a single verb call return a composed result the agent would otherwise assemble from many API calls.

Minimize the number of tools an MCP server exposes: every tool's name, description, parameter schema, and annotations load into the model's context on connect and tax reasoning before any prompt, and benchmark evidence shows task efficiency drops (>10 points) as tool-selection complexity rises. Consolidating many narrow tools into a few higher-level ones (e.g. 130+ to 11) can cut tool-definition context from roughly 26% to about 1.6%.
Filter out trivial tasks during curation: reject or redesign any task that can be completed without the MCP servers, or that MCP-equipped models solve consistently within five retries.

Design tasks around precise, objectively verifiable, multi-constraint requirements (exact counts, named waypoints, numeric thresholds, category filters) that require producing exact, inspectable end-state artifacts, so execution-based evaluators can deterministically check completion.
Cross-check every created task and every evaluator with independent reviewers for feasibility, ambiguity, and correctness before including it in the benchmark.

For dynamic, open-ended tasks with multiple valid solution paths, evaluate with an LLM-as-a-Judge that verifies completion against explicit key points, instead of exact tool-matching or fixed ground-truth trajectories.

Make evaluation robust to tool-use hallucination by decomposing the task into explicit completion criteria and grounding each key point against the raw tool outputs, rather than trusting the agent's self-reported completion or brittle rule-based/answer-based checks that do not scale in dynamic environments.
Define each evaluation key point to be atomic (one tool-mediated action), anchored to a concrete tool or observable signal, and auditable from logged inputs and outputs.
Build evals early in development, when product requirements translate naturally into test cases; waiting forces you to reverse-engineer success criteria from a live system.

Prefer execution-based evaluators (objective automated checks of structured outputs or end states) over LLM-as-a-judge whenever tasks depend on real-time or time-sensitive data, because a judge's static knowledge cannot assess time-varying answers and LLM judges carry style bias and hallucination.

Construct benchmark tasks with a two-stage human pipeline of separate proposers and validators, allowing LLM-assisted ideation only when each candidate task is human-vetted for authenticity, and having verifiers consolidate duplicates and check feasibility and execution quality.

Choose a strong judge model for LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation, and when any single evaluator's reliability is uncertain use multi-model majority voting; relative agent rankings are robust to evaluator bias even though absolute agreement varies by judge.

Record the limits of trajectory-based LLM evaluation: it retains residual model bias even after human-agreement validation, and it assumes tool descriptions reflect actual tool effects, an assumption that weakens as the toolset grows.

Score with multiple independent LLM judges, always report and pin the judge model version, report per-model cross-judge score ranges, and read small rank swaps within that band as evaluator uncertainty rather than capability differences.
Prefer structured claim-level scoring over holistic LLM-as-judge scoring, which introduces verbosity/style bias and reduces reproducibility.

Before trusting or deploying an LLM judge, run a reliability validation suite that stress-tests it with targeted perturbations rather than relying on a single point estimate of agreement with human raters on a small validation set.

Structure agent evaluators into three classes: format evaluators (output-format compliance), static evaluators (time-invariant content matching against manually collected answers), and dynamic evaluators (automatically retrieved real-time ground truth).

For temporally sensitive tasks, implement dynamic evaluators that recompute or re-fetch ground truth by invoking the same underlying data sources or APIs the task relies on, yielding checks that stay stable and reproducible across timestamps.

Report agent performance with multiple metrics (success rate, average evaluator/partial-credit score, and average steps) and assess both format compliance and content correctness under static and dynamic conditions, rather than success rate alone.
Treat a partial-credit (average-evaluator) score as diagnostic, not as a proxy for end-to-end success: a higher partial-credit score does not always predict a higher task success rate.
Do not equate more interaction steps with weaker capability: step efficiency varies independently of success rate, so judge efficiency and success separately.

Judge efficiency by execution steps on a cost-accuracy Pareto frontier rather than by model size: richer descriptions push most tasks to more steps, and a smaller model can dominate a larger one that spends more steps for equal or lower accuracy.

When selecting models for agent benchmarking, use top-ranked, high-capability models (e.g., top-ranked on a public arena and open-source models of at least 120B parameters) so results reflect frontier capability.

Expect and plan for the long-context challenge: input token count grows rapidly with interaction steps and can overflow context and degrade multi-step performance, concentrated in domains whose servers return large payloads (map data, full HTML, long financial series).
Expect a declarative natural-language interface to also cut pre-fill (prompt) token cost substantially, because query-construction context moves server-side instead of into the prompt.

Do not rely on naive per-step summarization of tool outputs to solve context growth: it improved results for some model/domain pairs but had no effect or hurt others, so validate any compression strategy per domain and model.

Mitigate the unknown-tools problem with an exploration phase in which the agent freely probes tool interfaces and constraints before an exploitation phase, but treat it as non-universal: it can fail to help or hurt, especially on tasks that require planning for state changes.
Optimize for the exploration-exploitation balance rather than raw tool-call volume: over-exploration yields diminishing returns and accumulates errors, while under-exploration fails to adapt.
Account for the cost of tool exploration: aggressive exploration substantially raises token consumption, so choose models and settings on the cost-versus-performance Pareto frontier.

Validate tool-call parameters against each tool's constraints before invoking it; a common failure is violating parameter rules such as setting identical start and end dates where the tool requires them to differ.

Diagnose wrong-tool selection, invalid or over-broad arguments, and unnecessary steps as a specification problem in the tool description, not a model bug, since defective, underspecified, or misleading descriptions directly cause these failures.
Validate tool (and prompt) inputs against their declared JSON schemas before execution, rather than trusting that schema-conformant declaration implies schema-conformant runtime payloads.

Evaluate tool selection and argument correctness as two separate aspects: selecting the correct tool is necessary but not sufficient, so score whether the model supplies correct arguments independently of whether it picked the right tool.

Do not assume an enterprise or product agent framework outperforms a plain ReAct loop: such frameworks can underperform, partly by relying on their internal tools instead of the task's designated MCP servers.

Match the agent architecture to the model: optimal agent-model pairing materially changes performance, and a specialized harness (e.g., a vendor Agent SDK) can substantially beat ReAct on the same backbone model.

Provide an alternative agent harness (e.g., an Agent SDK) for models with weak instruction-following that cannot reliably follow a ReAct output format, rather than forcing all models through one prompt scheme.

Expect cross-domain performance variance for a single model and optimize per domain rather than assuming uniform capability; tasks needing precise, multi-constraint tool use (e.g., navigation, repository management) tend to be hardest.
Direct agent improvement effort at content generation, which is the dominant failure source: models often exceed 80% on format compliance yet reach only 40-60% on content-sensitive checks.

When strict output format matters, account for reasoning-tuned models' weaker adherence to formatting instructions (a concrete failure is copying the prompt's format requirements verbatim without doing the task): add explicit format checks or format-robust parsing.

Explicitly test format invariance (blank lines, extra spaces, indentation), because judges are frequently more brittle to formatting than to semantic changes and formatting brittleness can distort downstream model comparisons and leaderboards even when meaning is unchanged.

Design agents to reason over partial information, adapt to diverse and unfamiliar tool interfaces, and handle ambiguous or failed tool responses gracefully, since real MCP tool use routinely presents all three.

Build the tool environment from stable, reproducible interfaces rather than unstable or simulated APIs: aggregate real MCP servers, drop any that require proprietary API keys, curate and vet for quality, and pin a dependency-free, containerized, security-checked toolset version.
Have annotators freely explore the toolset - its tool descriptions and real calls - to gain familiarity before proposing tasks or key points.

Formalize the setup as a single-turn, multi-call agentic task over real servers with a controlled, allow-listed tool exposure, a reference trajectory used only for analysis, and answer-centric claims scoring; model each tool as a typed relation returning either a well-typed value or an error token, and treat the interaction as a finite-horizon POMDP whose reward is attached post-hoc via claims scoring.

Treat each MCP tool description as the primary FM-facing interface the model uses to discover, select, parameterize, and orchestrate a tool; it is exposed to the FM alongside the tool name and input schema and directly shapes agent behavior.

Extract tool descriptions dynamically via the MCP reflection protocol (a tools/list request returns each tool's name, description, and input schema) rather than by static source parsing, so review and scanning work across any implementation language or proprietary server.

Advise MCP users to treat tool descriptions as mutable client-side configuration they can override at runtime without changing server code, using high-quality descriptions as a cost lever that can let a smaller, cheaper model reach parity with a larger one in a target domain before defaulting to a bigger model, since descriptions are a critical but under-engineered artifact best managed as a configurable engineering asset.

Evaluate and author every MCP tool description against a four-dimension quality standard — accuracy, functionality, information completeness, and conciseness — which together span 18 recurring description-smell categories.

When reviewing MCP tool handling, check tool identification (tools declared in the capabilities object with valid input/output schemas so they are discoverable and callable), tool execution (input types validated, execution terminates, runtime errors surfaced as error objects), and tool result propagation (result payload present, correctly structured, no success response masking a tool failure, no result-visibility races).

Treat an MCP tool's name, description, and parameter specification as the primary lever for correct tool selection: keep instructions simple and precise, and expect that even small description edits — tightening wording, adding/removing a tool, or merging similar tools — can move evaluation results significantly, while inaccurate descriptions cause wrong-tool choices, skipped steps, and malformed or missing arguments.
Prefer standardized MCP connectors over bespoke agent-to-system integrations when building agents that must reach many external tools or data sources.
Treat upfront loading of all MCP tool definitions as a scaling hazard, and design agents to disclose tool definitions only as needed.
Expose MCP tools as code interfaces in a navigable filesystem or equivalent API surface when an agent has a secure execution environment.
Give each agent a system prompt that clearly describes its role to reduce hallucination, and augment agents with external MCP tools and knowledge to mitigate reasoning errors.

Ship a companion skills layer alongside the tools that turns raw MCP tool access into guided, IDE-native, multi-step workflows, structured in three levels: an auto-loaded shared agent-instruction file per IDE, server-side prompt templates any client can invoke, and individual slash-command skills. This cuts the 3-5 exploratory calls an agent otherwise needs to learn a resource model and the token waste from failed calls and retries.

Embed the verifiable task constraints inside a realistic, natural-language user scenario so the agent must extract the operative requirements from conversational context rather than from a pre-structured specification.
Implement execution-based evaluators as code that returns a (pass/fail boolean, reason string) pair, so every failed check carries a diagnostic message explaining why it failed.
Seed the initial eval set from what you already test manually plus the bug tracker and support queue, converting real user-reported failures into test cases and prioritising by user impact.
Gate content checks behind a format check: an evaluator should first verify that required output keys are present and coercible to their expected types, and only then validate the values.
Gate CI/CD on the tool's process exit code (0 compliant, 1 non-compliant) and archive the --json-report output as the machine-readable validation evidence artifact.

For numeric answers, verify against a re-computed expected value within an explicit tolerance rather than requiring exact equality (e.g., fail only when the absolute difference exceeds a small threshold).
Standardize and report the experimental setup for reproducibility: fix decoding settings across all models (e.g., a common temperature) and pin the exact dated model version identifiers used.

Include tasks that require multi-hop reasoning over scattered clues to uniquely identify a target entity and report a specific identifier, exercising evidence aggregation rather than single-lookup retrieval.
Design tasks to be reasoning-intensive and multi-step, requiring the agent to resolve indirect references or filter datasets across multiple sources.

Structure a large-toolset agent as an adaptive decision loop with distinct Route (retrieve candidate tools), Execute (invoke a tool and observe feedback), and Response (finish) actions, rather than a fixed retrieve-then-execute pipeline, so it can re-route after errors and combine outputs across tools.

Prefer and reward active tool composition: agents that proactively interact with the tool environment (retrieving, executing, and combining multiple tools) succeed more than conservative agents that use roughly one tool per task.

Expect realistic large-scale toolsets to contain noisy or redundant tools: only a relevant subset is exercised by real tasks, so design retrieval and benchmarks to surface that subset rather than assuming every tool is needed.

Structure a large-toolset agent around two explicit operations - a retrieval (route) tool used as the discovery step when the model cannot solve the request alone or is unsure which tool to use, and an execution tool that may invoke only tools returned by the preceding route step and may retry a failing execution up to three times.

Apply the same embedding-retrieval mechanism beyond single-tool selection when scaling: agent selection (embed agent capability descriptions for two-level agent-then-tool routing), cross-organizational federated discovery (per-org indexes merged by a coordination layer preserving ownership and access control), and dynamic tool composition (mine the feedback loop for co-occurring tool chains to retrieve whole pipelines).

Route every downstream tool call through a client pool that discovers tools via tools/list at initialization and treats each tool as a pure function (name, params) -> result over its transport (stdio, SSE, or streamable-HTTP).
Score candidate tools during retrieval by combining server-level and tool-level similarity so that server-level priors dominate when the tool-level match is weak.

Structure the retrieval query with an explicit server-and-tool descriptor - server as the platform or permission domain and tool as the operation type plus target - and generate a concise server-level summary from each server's name, description, and tools to support server-level retrieval.
On complex, open-ended tasks the tool-result (retrieval) phase dominates the token budget across client types; large or retained tool outputs, not tool execution time, are the primary inflator.

Retrieve around five candidate tools per query: retrieving too few (k=1) significantly hurts success while increasing beyond five plateaus, and the tool-retrieval methodology - not the embedding model choice - is the dominant bottleneck, so invest there first.

Do not assume a retrieval-over-large-toolset method with a rigid pipeline is sufficient: prior approaches are limited by inflexible invocation and weak error recovery, and some by manually built, low-diversity toolsets.

Prioritize remediation by measured impact on tool selection — functionality first (+11.6%), then accuracy (+8.8%), then information completeness (+5.9%), then conciseness (+1.5%) — and adjust for query specificity: emphasize a clear, distinct functional description for underspecified queries and thorough completeness for detailed queries. Because the dimensions interact, improving one (for example adding parameter docs) can also improve another.

Choose retrieval parameters on accuracy grounds, because the token and latency savings are essentially free and domain-invariant: semantic filtering removes ~99% of tool-definition tokens across every server and K, and retrieval adds sub-100ms latency negligible next to LLM inference.

Diagnose agent failures into distinct categories - query errors (poor or wrong-granularity queries from weak task decomposition), retrieve errors (retriever misses a semantically equivalent tool), tool errors (correct tool invoked with wrong parameters), and other errors (unhandled transient failures) - and route each to its own remediation.

Build explicit error-handling into the agent framework - retries, failure recovery, and adaptive re-exploration - because agents that abandon a task on a transient failure (e.g., a network timeout) constitute a distinct and avoidable failure class.

Diagnose failures with a fixed 11-mode taxonomy split into a tool-call family (malformed parameters, wrong tool, no tool use, failed error recovery) and a cognitive family (task misunderstanding, faulty synthesis, misparsing, early termination, hallucination, logical error, constraint violation).

Treat tool-summary quality as a reliability dependency: most routing failures trace to ambiguous user queries or cryptic tool descriptions, so invest in clear, disambiguated, regenerated summaries and expect residual ambiguous-query cases to require clarification turns.

Treat large tool-invocation agents as a security surface: validate tools and monitor execution to guard against maliciously disguised tools and against destructive erroneous invocations such as unintended file deletion.
Treat misleading or incomplete tool descriptions as a security surface, not merely a usability issue: they can enable tool abuse, privilege escalation, and data exfiltration.

Treat MCP tools as untrusted and map each threat vector to its defense: prompt injection via image metadata to sanitization and semantic filters, schema bypass to strict enforcement and audit logs, remote code execution to capability scoping and sandboxing, privilege escalation to role-based tool binding, stale memory to TTL and garbage collection, cross-tool leakage to secure memory zones, provenance loss to output tagging, and command injection to input escaping.

Evaluate a tool-heavy agent on all three coupled failure modes of the Tools Tax - cost, reasoning degradation, and an enlarged tool-poisoning attack surface - not on token cost alone, because reducing in-context schemas improves all three at once.
Judge benchmark quality by domain coverage, generality, and compositional depth (multi-hop and cross-domain tasks) rather than by sheer task count.

Require benchmark tasks to satisfy three design principles: real-world relevance, temporal dynamics (time-sensitive tasks needing real-time retrieval rather than static internal knowledge), and tool diversity (needing integration of multiple tools rather than one sufficient tool).

Maintain task and harness quality through layered assurance (expert reference-trajectory execution, domain-expert correctness/solvability review, tool/server name-leakage review, automated claim-completeness verification, random-sample manual audit), and prefer systematic manual verification over automated task generation, which can compromise quality and naturalism.

For research agents, judge quality relative to the task by combining groundedness checks (claims supported by retrieved sources), coverage checks (key facts a good answer must include), and source-quality checks (authoritative, not merely first-retrieved sources), and frequently calibrate the LLM rubrics against expert human judgment.

Write unambiguous tasks: a good task is one where two domain experts would independently reach the same pass/fail verdict, and everything the grader checks is clear from the task description, so agents don't fail on ambiguous specs.

Verify a benchmark's claimed runtime dynamism by individually confirming that online-information tools fetch real data from live sources rather than returning simulated or pre-cached static responses.

Run evaluation against exclusively real, production servers rather than mocked substitutes so authentic error modes (rate limits, pagination, schema-version mismatches, transient errors) are exercised.
Pin and report the benchmark runtime environment, timeout, and transport mode (and note any per-server exceptions) so results are reproducible and comparable.

Report efficiency work reproducibly and honestly: fix seeds, release a no-API token-counting harness, validate on a community-standard benchmark rather than only synthetic (even if calibrated) workloads, and explicitly mark projected downstream metrics as extrapolations to be verified against live agents.

Use a uniform non-zero decoding temperature (around 0.7) across models for long-horizon agent evaluation to mitigate suboptimal greedy decoding in reasoning models, since sporadic randomness has negligible cumulative impact on aggregate performance.

Select the evaluation metric to match the question: single-run success rate as the primary metric, pass@k to assess the ability to discover diverse solution paths, and pass^k to assess consistency and reliability.

Select the aggregate metric by what matters: use pass@k (probability of at least one correct solution in k attempts; rises with k) when only one success is needed (e.g. pass@1 for coding), and pass^k (probability all k trials succeed; falls with k) for customer-facing agents needing consistent, reliable behaviour every time.
Pin a specific recommended judge model (e.g., DeepSeek-V3-0324) for reproducible results, while allowing substitution by models with higher human agreement or more robust frameworks.
Treat judge reliability as a joint property of the whole configuration — model, rubric, and prompt template — and report that reliability alongside the benchmark results the judge produces.
Evaluate all candidate judges on the same fixed, curated synthetic test set per benchmark so that judge comparisons are made on identical inputs.

Do not assume any single judge is uniformly reliable, or that the largest or most expensive model is the best judge; benchmark cost against reliability, since a smaller, cheaper open model can match or beat premium frontier judges at a fraction of the inference cost.
Adopt reliability-aware judge selection, reporting, and benchmarking: identify and rule out unreliable judge configurations before they influence model comparisons or safety evaluations.

Treat tool-use hallucination as real but low-prevalence and largely detectable (about 9% of invocations, ~1.6% evaluation inconsistency, detection stable across judges), while still guarding the known weak spot: evaluators overlook critical details in excessively long, complex trajectories.
Consider per-step, agent-based assessment of each trajectory step to close the long-trajectory evaluation blind spot, but weigh it against the significant loss of evaluation efficiency it incurs.

Examine the agent trajectory turn-by-turn for progression signals: forward progress versus looping on the same call, adaptive versus identical retry after an error, unproductive tool switching when one correct tool was available, and stopping while required data is still missing.

Normalize collected key points into a canonical set: imperative voice, one action per point, explicit inter-step dependencies, and deduplication of paraphrases, keeping the coarsest level that stays auditable without hiding required tool interactions.
Use LLM-generated key points as a reliable substitute for human-annotated ones when human annotations are unavailable, since both capture similar critical steps despite differing in ordering.

Instruct the evaluation judge to fail a task when required information came from the model's internal knowledge rather than an actual tool call, and to require file creation for tasks that specify it.
Require every task to be tool-dependent and stable: it must need external data to solve and rely on information that stays valid throughout the evaluation window.

Author evaluation prompts as single-turn natural language that never name any server, tool, or parameter, avoid subjective phrasing, and never reveal internal mechanics or the solution path, so the agent must infer the tool chain itself.

Evaluate and author tool descriptions in terms of six components (Purpose, Usage Guidelines, Limitations, Parameter Explanation, Length & Completeness, Examples), grouped into requirement-like specification components (Purpose, Limitations, Parameter Explanation, Examples) and prompt-like instructional components (Usage Guidelines, Length & Completeness).

When automatically scoring tool descriptions, apply a well-defined analytic rubric (more consistent than open-ended prompts) via a multi-model LLM jury drawn from disparate model families to mitigate single-model bias; such rubric scoring aligns with human judgment at substantial agreement.

Score final answers against a list of atomic, independently verifiable claims grounded in tool outputs and decoupled from any specific trajectory, so any valid tool-call path that yields the same claims gets full credit.

Release a public split with, per task, the task id, enabled tool list, natural-language prompt, grounded claims, and reference trajectory — the trajectory supporting reproducibility, smoke tests, solvability audits, and diagnostics but never used as a scoring target.
Score each claim on a three-level scale (fulfilled=1.0, partial=0.5, not=0.0), take task coverage as the mean claim score, and pass at a fixed coverage threshold such as 0.75.
Populate every task's exposed tool set with plausible, semantically-similar distractor tools so the evaluation tests tool discovery under noise, not just execution with a known API.

Construct each task's tool environment for sufficiency (the minimum necessary relevant tools) plus plausible-but-irrelevant distractors, and for multi-source tasks require combining evidence across tool families without introducing unnecessary ambiguity.

Containerize every server with a sandboxed read-only filesystem (except explicit writable work dirs), allow-listed network egress, a version-pinned image digest, and a restart between tasks to guarantee reproducibility and prevent cross-task state leakage.
Pin server container versions, publish re-scoring runs when upstream drift is detected, and treat trajectory-level reproducibility as bounded by upstream service stability.

Evaluate all models under matched task-level conditions (same prompt, tool set, budget, rubric, final-answer protocol) with no model-specific demonstrations, retries, or scaffolding, while still following a provider's recommended native tool-calling strategy where one exists.
Ship each task with a reference trajectory (a gold-standard sequence of calls with rationales) and a grounded final answer that is strictly supported by tool outputs.
Allow a bounded number of per-task retries with tool-error summaries fed back into the model context for fairness, and permit partial-response grading when the model reaches the tool-call limit.

When building tasks to ground or evaluate a tool, write self-contained plain-English questions with a single unambiguous answer reachable in one tool call, specifying all inputs, varying values across tasks, and spanning medium/hard/very-hard difficulty; then synthesize Examples and Limitations strictly from the observed executions, each example a real observation with exact arguments and response (preferring edge and error cases) and each limitation a tool-specific fact seen in a trace, never invented, never generic API advice, and never a verbatim repeat of the description.
Fix an explicit per-task tool-call budget; relaxing it is expected to raise absolute scores but not to change relative rankings.

Expect cognitive failures to dominate once basic tool mechanics are solved: the bottleneck moves to deciding when enough evidence is gathered and synthesizing the answer, so target claim-aware stopping criteria and trajectory-grounded verification of the answer against collected evidence.

Watch for a tool-use policy mismatch in which reasoning-trained models emit no tool calls on tasks that require external evidence, and treat frequent no-tool-use as a calibration failure rather than a capability limit.
Use reference trajectories only for solvability checks, tool-dependence validation, and post-hoc diagnostics — never for pass/fail scoring.
Mitigate reference-trajectory path bias in diagnostics by using claim-based pass/fail scoring, diagnosing only after a failure, and treating the trajectory as one sufficient evidence trace.
Reserve a held-out private split for exposure monitoring and leaderboard integrity, and report public-private split gaps as audit signals rather than direct evidence of memorization or contamination.
Report 95% confidence intervals via nonparametric bootstrap over per-task coverage scores, and expect residual claim-list noise to bound the achievable pass rate even for a perfect agent.
Apply flexible numerical matching when scoring claims — approximation thresholds scaled to the domain, with mathematically equivalent expressions treated as matches.

Select servers by explicit criteria: stable, well-documented implementations; diversity across functional categories; multiple related tools per server to enable meaningful distractors; and applicability to realistic multi-step workflows.
In agentic latency analysis attribute wall-clock time primarily to tool-call roundtrip latency, not model inference, and do not assume a smaller ('Mini') model is faster end-to-end.

Mitigate the risks of live tool-use evaluation — sandbox containers, restrict egress, withhold the private split, exclude secrets from releases, document upstream licenses, and release derived claims/scores rather than raw snapshots — and position the benchmark as a diagnostic instrument, not a safety certification for high-stakes deployment.
Invoke the evaluator judge once per claim (an independent call per claim) rather than once per task, to avoid loss-of-context problems on tasks with many claims.
Run the failure-diagnosis prompt only for task-model pairs whose coverage is below the pass threshold, and use the resulting labels for post-hoc analysis only, never for pass/fail scoring.

Report a diagnostic profile — accuracy, efficiency, judge sensitivity, split gap, drift, and failure mode — rather than a single pass rate, and add multi-turn clarification and distractor ablations to the evaluation.
State the language and locale scope of the benchmark explicitly (for example, English-only prompts bound the conclusions and exclude non-English tool use, script handling, and localization failures).
Specify every evaluation benchmark as a triple: the input (a natural-language user request), the expected tools to be called, and the expected arguments for each tool.
Include the reference trajectory in the diagnostic prompt as a verified evidence trace (not a target policy) so the diagnostic judge can localize failures against the missed claims.

Instruct the diagnostic judge to localize a failure relative to the missed claims and to never penalize alternative valid plans, different tool orderings, extra or parallel calls, or different parameterizations that produce the same claim-supporting evidence.

Structure the diagnostic prompt in ordered stages: anchor on the ground-truth trajectory and expected claims, examine the actual agent behavior, consider which claims were missed and why (using the scorer's per-claim reasoning as evidence), then map to a failure mode.

In failure diagnosis assign one primary failure mode (the one best explaining the coverage gap) plus contributing modes from the same fixed vocabulary, mark a mode as root cause only when it caused downstream failures, calibrate diagnostic confidence explicitly, and resolve tricky boundaries with explicit disambiguation rules.
Use one shared set of failure-mode definitions for both human reviewers and the automated diagnostic judge to keep classification consistent.

Treat the coverage threshold as a reporting decision (the rubric returns a real-valued coverage score), report mean coverage and pass rate at several thresholds, and expect model rankings to be largely preserved across thresholds.
Provide a credential-free local smoke test so the evaluation harness can be exercised without provider API keys.

Release the dataset under an open license and the harness/evaluator code under a permissive license; because third-party servers and tool outputs carry upstream terms, release only curated claim-audit snippets and derived scores rather than complete raw tool-output snapshots.
Budget evaluator cost as the number of trajectories times the mean claims per task (since judging is per-claim), and multiply by the number of judges for a cross-judge sensitivity study.
Evaluate the agent as the harness (scaffold) and model working together, not the model in isolation, because the two jointly determine agent behaviour.

Grade the outcome (the final state in the environment at the end of a trial), not what the transcript claims the agent did; verify the real end state (e.g. the reservation exists in the database) rather than trusting a success message.

Read transcripts and grades from many trials regularly and invest in transcript-viewing tooling, because you cannot know whether graders work without doing so; a failed-task transcript reveals whether the agent made a genuine mistake or the grader rejected a valid solution.
Run multiple trials per task rather than a single run, because model outputs vary between runs and repetition yields more consistent, reliable measurement.
Treat evals as a high-bandwidth communication channel between product and research: eval tasks define the concrete metrics researchers can optimise against.

Without evals, teams debug reactively and cannot distinguish real regressions from noise, test changes at scale before shipping, or measure improvement; good evals make behavioural changes visible before they reach users.

Enable the people closest to requirements and users (product managers, customer success, salespeople) to contribute eval tasks directly (e.g. as a PR), since they are best positioned to define success.

Understand each evaluation method's trade-offs before relying on it: automated evals give fast, reproducible, no-user-impact iteration but need maintenance and can create false confidence; production monitoring gives ground truth but is reactive and noisy; A/B testing measures real outcomes and controls confounds but is slow and needs traffic; user feedback surfaces unanticipated problems but is sparse and skewed; manual transcript review builds intuition but doesn't scale; human studies are gold-standard but expensive and slow.

Choose grader types by trade-off: prefer deterministic code-based graders where possible (fast, cheap, reproducible, but brittle to valid variation), use model-based graders where flexibility or nuance is needed (scalable but non-deterministic and needing calibration), and use human graders judiciously for validation (gold standard but expensive and slow).
Score multidimensional success by combining graders per task—weighted (combined score must hit a threshold), binary (all must pass), or hybrid—rather than relying on a single check.

Set target pass rates by eval purpose: capability ('quality') evals should start at a low pass rate on tasks the agent struggles with, while regression evals should sit near 100% so any decline signals breakage.
Once an agent is launched and optimised, graduate high-pass-rate capability evals into a regression suite run continuously to catch drift.

Treat a 0% pass rate across many trials with frontier models (e.g. 0% pass@100) as most likely a broken task or grader, not an incapable agent, and investigate the eval before concluding the agent failed.

Watch for saturation: an eval at 100% pass rate tracks regressions but gives no signal for improvement, and near saturation large capability gains show up as small score increases (e.g. SWE-Bench Verified moved from ~30% to >80% within a year), so retire or refresh saturated evals for capability measurement.

For conversational agents, evaluate the interaction itself: combine verifiable end-state outcomes, transcript constraints (e.g. finished under N turns), and LLM rubrics for task completion and interaction quality, often using a second LLM to simulate the user across multi-turn dialogue.

Build agentic-transcript perturbations with a staged LLM pipeline — plan the edit steps, apply them coherently with an editor that accounts for preceding turns, consolidate state with a summarizer, and confirm the target outcome with an optional verifier — so each edit stays logically consistent with the rest of the transcript.

Evaluate computer-use and browser-use agents in a real or sandboxed environment, verifying the intended outcome through backend state rather than a confirmation page, and check that the agent selects the right interaction mode (DOM-based is fast but token-heavy; screenshot-based is slower but more token-efficient).

Start small: begin with as few as 20-50 simple tasks drawn from real observed failures rather than waiting for hundreds, because early on each system change has a large, noticeable effect so small samples suffice.
Create a reference solution—a known working output that passes all graders—for each task to prove the task is solvable and to verify the graders are configured correctly.
Make graders resistant to bypasses and hacks so that passing genuinely requires solving the problem rather than exploiting unintended loopholes.
Build balanced problem sets that test both where a behaviour should occur and where it should not, to avoid class-imbalanced evals and the one-sided optimisation they cause.

Build a robust harness with a stable environment and isolate each trial by starting from a clean state, because unnecessary shared state (leftover files, cached data, prior git history, resource exhaustion) causes correlated failures or inflated performance and makes results unreliable.

Grade what the agent produced, not the specific path it took (e.g. an exact tool-call sequence), because checking rigid step sequences yields brittle tests that punish valid approaches the eval designer didn't anticipate.
For tasks with multiple components, build in partial credit so an agent that completes some steps scores above one that fails immediately, giving finer-grained signal.

Apply the constant fundamentals across all agent types: start early, source realistic tasks from observed failures, define unambiguous and robust success criteria, design graders thoughtfully by combining multiple types, make problems hard enough for the model, iterate to improve signal-to-noise, and read the transcripts.

Calibrate LLM-as-judge graders against human experts, give the judge an explicit way out (e.g. return 'Unknown' when it lacks information) to avoid hallucination, and use clear structured rubrics that grade each dimension with an isolated judge rather than one judge for all dimensions.
When grading free-form answers at scale, use an LLM judge that returns a binary correct/incorrect verdict on whether the prediction covers the ground-truth key information.

Double-check tasks and graders before trusting low scores, because subtle failure modes—grading bugs, agent-harness constraints, or ambiguity—can produce low scores despite good agent performance (e.g. a model rose from 42% to 95% on CORE-Bench after fixing rigid grading, ambiguous specs, and non-reproducible tasks).
Design evals so failures seem fair—it is clear what the agent got wrong and why—so that when scores don't climb you can be confident it is due to agent performance and not a broken eval.

Do not take eval scores at face value until someone digs into the details and reads transcripts; if grading is unfair, tasks are ambiguous, valid solutions are penalised, or the harness constrains the model, revise the eval before trusting it.

Treat the eval suite as a living artifact with clear ownership: a durable model is a dedicated evals team owning core infrastructure while domain experts and product teams contribute most tasks and run the evaluations themselves.

Make owning and iterating on evaluations as routine as maintaining unit tests, because teams can waste weeks on AI features that 'work' in early testing but fail unstated expectations a good eval would surface early.

Practice eval-driven development: define eval tasks that express planned capabilities before the agent can fulfil them, then iterate until it performs well; defining the tasks also stress-tests whether product requirements are concrete enough to build, and low starting pass rates make progress on bets visible.

Map evaluation methods to lifecycle stages: automated evals pre-launch and in CI/CD, production monitoring post-launch for drift, A/B testing to validate significant changes once traffic suffices, ongoing user-feedback triage and weekly transcript sampling, and reserve systematic human studies for calibrating LLM graders or evaluating subjective outputs.

Structure the offline evaluation pipeline as three stages — fulfillment (run each benchmark across multiple models with the full tool list supplied, recording invoked tools and arguments), evaluation (compute metrics and scores from the raw outputs), and summarization (aggregate dataset-level statistics into a final report).

Layer multiple evaluation methods like a Swiss-cheese safety model, because no single layer catches every issue; the most effective teams pair automated evals for iteration, production monitoring for ground truth, and periodic human review for calibration.
Choose an eval framework that fits your workflow quickly, then invest your energy in high-quality test cases and graders, because frameworks are only as good as the tasks run through them.

Do not assume an MCP server outperforms an equivalent function-call/tool-use implementation on accuracy; MCP wrapping alone yields no measured accuracy gain, so justify MCP adoption by other benefits (standardization, interoperability) rather than expected accuracy.

Evaluate an MCP server on three axes together — answer accuracy, end-to-end latency, and token consumption — not accuracy alone, because efficiency and cost vary more sharply across servers than accuracy does.

Expect a wide performance spread across MCP servers (measured accuracy ~10-64%, latency <15s to ~231s) and select a server by benchmarking candidates on your own task instead of trusting popularity or defaults.

Verify MCP servers at the protocol-runtime level, not only at build time: a server can compile successfully and conform to its specification yet still violate its coordination obligations at runtime, so build success and spec conformance do not imply correct runtime behavior.
Choose a code-execution MCP architecture only when the expected token, latency, privacy, or composition gains justify the added infrastructure and security cost.

Profile MCP at the protocol level rather than as an end-to-end black box: standardization removes n-by-m integration glue but adds schema-discovery, injection, and context-management overhead that answer-level benchmarks miss and that affects latency and tokens even when answer quality is unchanged.

Wrap each MCP server as an HTTP-exposed FaaS function (e.g. a Lambda Function URL), because MCP's stdio/local transports cannot be embedded directly in a function; this mimics a remote MCP server, gains FaaS scaling, and isolates tool execution for security.

Frame the CLI-versus-MCP choice as a question of tool design, not of protocol: the token-cost gap benchmarks attribute to MCP comes from tool-schema bloat and naive one-tool-per-endpoint design, so a well-designed MCP server removes the cost argument against MCP without giving up its advantages.
For stdio servers, separate the target server command with a `--` so mcp-validate does not consume the server's own flags (required for npx and similar wrapped commands).

Report accuracy over valid samples (those that completed the full pipeline and were logged) and track infrastructure failures separately, so network/API-key/crash losses are not confused with poor answer quality.

Scope effectiveness evaluation to data-fetching MCPs, whose accuracy is directly measurable, and treat world-changing MCPs separately because verifying their effect requires inspecting post-action state you may not be able to access.
MCP feature scope: the tier audit scores 48 non-experimental features (36 core, 6 transport, 6 protocol); the 5 Tasks features are experimental and informational and do not count.
Reduce dataset bias in a retrieval/search benchmark by spanning multiple languages and knowledge domains rather than a single homogeneous source.

Prefer a declarative natural-language interface over a raw structured-query parameter, moving query construction (e.g. text-to-SQL) inside the server; the gain is large when the LLM's query construction is the accuracy bottleneck (PostgreSQL +22 points) and small when it is not (MySQL +2 points).
Treat the format and content a server returns to the LLM as a first-class design decision: it directly gates whether the LLM can answer correctly.

Return results processed enough to be directly usable, but keep the underlying source detail — raw unprocessed dumps force the LLM into error-prone guesswork, while summarize-only output that hides the originals leaves no recovery path when the server's own analysis is wrong.

Avoid silently truncating results or returning snippets too thin to answer with; truncation can drop the correct span and insufficient descriptions force a second fetch, both degrading accuracy and efficiency.

Design every tool description to serve a dual role: a requirement-like specification of the tool's expected behavior and parameter constraints, and a prompt-like instruction that guides the FM's reasoning about when and how to invoke it.

Do not write Examples or the full Limitations from the description alone; ground them in observed tool executions by generating at least one success task and one error task per tool plus edge cases (prioritizing harder cases first), because an FM cannot reliably infer them without traces and augmentation must preserve the tool's original meaning and intent.

Give every tool input an explicit argument name and state its data type and expected format (for example yyyy-mm-dd) so the FM issues correctly bounded calls instead of defaulting to broad parameters that inflate tool-response size and token cost.

Ensure every tool description clearly states its purpose (the function, behavior, and return data), guides the FM on when and how to use the tool, and includes relevant caveats; a bare purpose statement without behavioral or output detail is only minimally viable.

Account for tool metadata being repeatedly injected into the FM context on every interaction: excessive detail saturates the context window and raises cost, so any augmentation must justify its token cost and seek compact representations.

Assume tool-description quality is poor by default and always review it: in a large empirical study 97.1% of descriptions carried at least one smell and 56% failed to state purpose clearly, where a smell is a recurring component-specific pattern that degrades clarity, correctness, or maintainability without being an outright fault.

Prioritize the most prevalent smells when reviewing descriptions: Unstated Limitations (~90%), Missing Usage Guidelines (~89%), and Opaque Parameters (~84%) dominate, only ~2.9% of descriptions are fully smell-free, and completeness drops sharply as more components are required, so most descriptions lack boundary conditions, when/how-to-use guidance, and parameter insight.

Do not assume a description is good because it comes from an official server or reputable vendor: quality shows no significant official-vs-community difference (23 official and 80 community servers were comparably smelly), and minimal one-line descriptions that merely restate the tool name are below-median quality.

Interpret a rubric smell as a potential risk signal, not a deterministic predictor of failure: whether a missing component actually hurts depends on tool complexity, task difficulty, available context budget, and the model's prior exposure to the tool, API, or domain.

Treat tool descriptions as first-class engineering artifacts: run rubric-based smell detection in review or CI as a blocking release criterion, fix the highest-leverage components first, add examples or exhaustive parameter detail only where they justify their token cost, and use manual refinement for small servers but reviewed semi-automated augmentation for large ones, always resolving ambiguity without inflating the token footprint past its efficiency payoff.

Because description quality is systemically poor and cannot be reliably delegated to individual teams, support ecosystem-level gating: registries and marketplaces should scan published servers and surface smell summaries, quality badges, and threshold warnings, analogous to security advisories in package registries.

Score each component on a graded (5-point) scale rather than a yes/no check, treating 3 as the minimum viable threshold, 4-5 as increasing precision and clarity, and a mean below 3 as a detected smell, because a component can be present yet semantically ambiguous or sub-optimal.

Map each below-threshold component deterministically to its smell (Unclear Purpose, Missing Usage Guidance, Unstated Limitation, Opaque Parameters, Underspecified or Incomplete, Exemplar Issues); no separate heuristic or classifier is needed to name the defect.

Treat augmentation gains as real but neither free nor universal: augmenting all components raised task success by about 5.85 percentage points (median) and partial-goal completion by about 15.12%, but increased execution steps by about 67.46% (median) and regressed roughly 16.67% of cases.

Apply augmentation adaptively per domain and model rather than uniformly: gains improved roughly 54% of runs but regressed roughly 17%, help is largest in some domains and negative in others, and richer descriptions raise partial-goal completion even when final success is capped by an iteration limit.

Budget for augmentation's cost side: median execution steps rose about 67% and token usage rose materially (about +22-41% input, +11-69% output), though the penalty is not universal, since a smaller model reduced its steps while still improving success and evaluator scores.

Prefer shorter, targeted descriptions that preserve the core semantic content: no single component combination performs best everywhere, compact variants often match full augmentation while cutting tokens, and removing Examples typically does not degrade performance.

Drop the Examples component first when trimming a description: removing it did not significantly degrade performance and even slightly improved cross-domain consistency, consistent with Anthropic's deprioritization though contrary to generic few-shot expectations; keep examples only where a tool is unfamiliar or complex enough to benefit.

Where you influence protocol or server design, expose description components as structured fields rather than one monolithic text blob, so agents can assemble the most effective, budget-appropriate description profile at runtime.

Do not assume that Agent Skills (progressive discovery) or Tool Search (on-demand lookup) remove the need for good tool descriptions; they reduce context loading but the FM still relies on descriptions to select and invoke tools.
Always include the Purpose component in a tool description and in any pruned component subset, because without it the FM cannot infer what the tool does or when to use it.

Apply the same description-quality discipline to Agent Skill metadata: because progressive disclosure loads only the Skill's name and summary at startup to decide activation, that description metadata determines whether the correct Skill is discovered, so author it with the same accuracy, functionality, completeness, and conciseness rigor.

Produce the augmented description as five explicit component fields (Purpose, Guidelines, Limitations, Parameter Explanation, Examples); do not add a separate Length & Completeness field, because it is a meta-quality dimension automatically satisfied when the other five are well populated.

When the context budget is tight, prune Parameter Explanation before other components: the MCP input schema already supplies parameter names and types at runtime, the component often duplicates that information, and including every component can otherwise inflate context and reduce efficiency.

Treat Examples as the lowest-priority component and the safest to omit under constraints: their value is contested, they scored only moderate inter-rater reliability, and they can be too large to fit the context window.

Measure a description change with execution-based metrics rather than assuming its effect: Success Rate, Average Evaluator score (partial completion), and Average Steps as a cost proxy, using a benchmark that combines programmatic evaluators with LLM judgment; a Tool Description Router can swap description variants at runtime to run these comparisons without changing server code, and augmentation reliably lifts rubric scores whose task-level payoff must still be measured.

Weigh underspecification as a real reliability risk, not a cosmetic issue: under-specified prompts have caused up to 2x performance regressions across model versions, so pervasive description smells plausibly increase agent brittleness.
Use a description that conveys purpose, usage guidelines, limitations, and parameters together as the positive exemplar of quality, rather than a one-line stub.

Hold each component to its quality bar: Usage Guidelines state when to use and when not to use (plus disambiguation if the name is ambiguous); Limitations state what the tool does not return and its scope and constraints; Parameter Explanation gives each parameter's type, meaning, behavioral effect, and required-or-default status rather than schema-only listing; the prose is self-sufficient with examples supplementing rather than replacing it and roughly four or more substantive sentences; judge a description Bad if any component is below viable or examples replace the description, and Good only if all components are at least minimally viable.

Select the minimal effective component set for each domain-model pair, always retaining Purpose: there is no universal 'golden' combination, but a pruned combination that keeps the core purpose and the most relevant constraints solves largely the same tasks as full augmentation (strong statistical agreement) while cutting tokens and latency, provided the pruning is tailored to the domain.

Write components as precise behavioral constraints (valid input ranges, temporal offsets, concrete rules) and remove ambiguous, contradictory, or self-referential statements, which degrade agent performance and dilute otherwise-useful guidance when combined with other components.

For Accuracy, keep the description semantically consistent with the implementation: describe only behaviors the tool actually has, declare the behaviors it does have, state its behavioral boundaries, and give each parameter's correct type and meaning, so the agent neither invokes non-existent behavior nor misreads argument constraints.

For mission-critical tasks where accuracy outweighs cost, consider running the failures of one description configuration through an alternative configuration, since full and pruned descriptions solve overlapping but partially distinct task sets and neither subsumes the other.

Scale description depth to need: a direct, compact description suffices when the model already knows the tool, API, or domain or the task is simple, while unfamiliar domains, complex tasks, or tools with subtle invocation constraints warrant fully augmented descriptions to bridge the comprehension gap.

Ground FM-based augmentation in implementation evidence: supply the tool's source-code slice together with the original description and input schema and instruct the model to invent nothing unsupported, because underspecified inputs otherwise lead the augmentor to hallucinate fluent but inconsistent details, especially for the prompt-generated Purpose, Guidelines, and Parameter Explanation.

Expect source-code grounding to improve description faithfulness and rubric-scoring reliability most for behavior- and input-tied components, particularly Parameter Explanation, by correcting the lower-scoring, hallucinating cases.

Adopt source-code grounding as a reliability safeguard rather than a guaranteed performance optimization: it may not change task success for tools well represented in training data, but it unlocks some otherwise-failing cases and matters most for rare, proprietary, or out-of-distribution tools.

When deploying augmented descriptions, enforce explicit resource caps (maximum steps, thinking budget, rate and token limits) tuned per domain, allowing higher caps where success gains justify the overhead and lower caps or compact configurations where gains are small or negative, because richer descriptions inflate execution cost.

Recognize that behaviorally precise cues, not sheer metadata volume, drive tool and skill discoverability: structured components enable lazy loading (request Purpose for initial selection, load guidelines or examples only on invocation), and weak or missing critical cues rather than metadata size likely explain progressive-disclosure discoverability failures.

To cut multi-step loop cost, consider code-mode or programmatic tool execution, where the model generates orchestration code so intermediate tool responses are not round-tripped back through the model, reducing both steps and tokens.

Recommend the design-once/execute-many pattern when a multi-step tool task recurs: per-execution cost falls to roughly O(1) (about 150 tokens), the one-time design cost breaks even after only ~4% of a single agent run, and amortized token savings exceed 99% past about five executions; treat the specific savings figures as conservative, estimated lower bounds rather than exact per-model measurements.

Treat the tool description, together with its name and input schema, as the primary and often only basis an LLM has for selecting a tool: implementation is unobservable, so selection is driven by the semantic alignment between the query and the description.
Make tool discovery text explicit: use capability-specific names and descriptions, and tell the model what broad tool domains can be searched.

Do not statically expose the entire tool catalog to the LLM; retrieve only a small, semantically relevant subset (typically 3-5 tools) per query via dense-embedding similarity search. Static provisioning wastes tokens (a 100-tool catalog is ~20K-80K tokens before any query), degrades accuracy through context bloat, and hits context-window limits; manual curation is inflexible.

Replace eager, uniform injection of every tool schema with dynamic, query-conditioned tool selection: load only the tools whose intent matches the current turn, mirroring how attention lets each position attend only to what matters.

Make tool summaries self-documenting and query-shaped: descriptive names and intent-voiced summaries substantially raise retrieval quality, and an LLM can regenerate cryptic implementer-voiced summaries to be shorter yet more retrievable.

Architect dynamic tool access around three tools - search_tools (semantic search plus a tool-category overview), describe_tools (on-demand schemas), and execute_tool - so that discoverability and token efficiency are both achieved.

Separate schema retrieval (describe_tools) from tool search so input schemas load only for the tools the LLM will actually use, since input schemas are the dominant token cost (often 60-80% of a static toolset's tokens).

Put an overview of the available tool categories into the tool-search description so the LLM knows what exists and will actually attempt a search; pure semantic search fails when the model has no visibility into what tools are available.

For Functionality, make the tool distinct within a shared namespace: give it a unique, semantically meaningful name (not a generic utility name such as read_file or get_data), a clear functional description, and explicit trigger conditions stating when this tool should be prioritized over similar tools.

For Information Completeness, document everything the agent needs to build a valid call and interpret the result without guessing: every parameter and its type, the return values, side effects, and error handling; omitting return-value descriptions forces zero-shot output handling and invites hallucination.

For Conciseness, maximize signal-to-noise: remove redundant or repeated content, irrelevant clutter, needless technical jargon, and useless qualifiers, because verbosity inflates token cost and dilutes model attention — while treating conciseness as the lowest-impact of the four dimensions.

Diagnose tool-selection failures by mode: an under-specific or vague description causes missed invocation (the correct tool is not selected), whereas an over-general or ambiguous description causes erroneous selection (a wrong tool is chosen); remediate by increasing specificity and disambiguating.
Write descriptions for machine reasoning under context-window limits rather than for human readers; concise, well-structured descriptions reduce hallucination and improve tool-selection accuracy.

Also avoid vague hedge words (for example maybe or probably), keep terminology consistent, and keep wording understandable to the model; these general documentation qualities matter, but for short MCP descriptions they are secondary to the four core dimensions and were not among the mapped MCP smells.

Expect substantial, measurable payoff from a standards-compliant description: among functionally equivalent competitors, a compliant server wins selection about 72% of the time versus a 20% uniform baseline (a 260% relative increase), consistently across domains and query-complexity levels.

Treat description authoring as a first-class engineering phase, co-equal with implementation and testing (like API contract design); avoid the code-first, description-last pattern, which measurably degrades tool discoverability and invocation accuracy.
Keep tool descriptions synchronized with the implementation as code evolves: a description accurate at authoring time drifts stale after code updates, and static checks do not catch this drift.

Detect MCP faults behaviorally, not only via crashes or explicit errors: many faults return well-formed JSON-RPC success responses while violating coordination semantics (silent/gray failure), so oracles must assert response content, session-state consistency, and the occurrence of required notification events across interaction steps.

Use the 27 fault subcategories as a structured fault-localization checklist for diagnostic triage, narrowing an MCP server misbehavior to protocol-level hypotheses such as Schema Compatibility, Session State, or Tool Result Propagation.

Derive MCP conformance tests and fault-injection scenarios directly from the leaf fault categories (for example, verifying that timeout violations yield structured error objects, undeclared tool identifiers are rejected, and requests are not processed before initialization completes), and ground reliability benchmarks in observed protocol-level faults rather than generic software bugs.

Push recurring MCP correctness checks into SDK and protocol infrastructure (default tool-input validation, request-response identifier propagation, prevention of premature request handling, and helpers for structured JSON-RPC error objects) instead of re-fixing the same fault classes in each implementation.

When reviewing MCP Base Protocol handling, check message structure (required JSON-RPC 2.0 fields id/method/params/result/error present and propagated, with correct request-response id correlation) and message semantics (identifiers consistent across related events; failures represented as structured error objects, not HTTP status codes).

When reviewing the MCP session lifecycle, check initialization (protocol version match, no capability-negotiation races, initialized notifications sent, no use of uninitialized state), state transition (correct async control flow, no requests before initialization completes), and termination (correct shutdown ordering, resource release, input streams closed).

Isolate domain-specific faults with a domain relevance filter rather than relying on generic bug labels and fault keywords alone (which were 80% false positives for MCP), and analyze full issue-centered threads rather than titles or labels because the confirming evidence often appears only in diagnostic comments, linked pull requests, commit messages, or closing discussions.
Diagnose MCP vision composition failures at the protocol layer (schema semantics, memory scoping, runtime coordination) rather than attributing them to individual model or tool errors.

Represent tool and server failures as structured JSON-RPC error objects mapped to the correct error code; never return a success response that carries hidden failure information, and never surface application failures as bare HTTP status codes.

Treat a failing tool as an ordinary result with `is_error=True` (the exception message is placed in `content` for the model), always check `is_error` before trusting `structured_content` (which is `None` on failure), and remember a Client method raises `MCPError` only when the server returns a JSON-RPC error rather than a result.

Gate request handling on completion of the initialization handshake so no request is processed before the session is fully initialized; because initialization instability spans several startup steps, expect to harden the whole startup sequence rather than a single step.
Preserve request-response and session identifiers consistently across message exchange, tool invocation, and result propagation, so requests, results, and related streaming events stay correlated.

Keep diagnostic and other non-protocol output off the JSON-RPC message stream; on the stdio transport, emitting anything other than valid JSON-RPC on standard output corrupts the stream and breaks client parsing.

When reviewing MCP transport handling, check the stdio binding (only valid JSON-RPC 2.0 emitted on standard output) and the Streamable HTTP binding (correct handling of HTTP requests, session identifiers, and server-sent event streams, including request throttling under high-volume traffic).
Keep protocol and diagnostics separate on stdio: log to stderr (captured automatically by the host) and never write log output to stdout, which carries protocol messages.

Set operation timeouts adaptively to workload and handle cancellation and stream-termination correctly, so long-running or streaming operations are neither terminated prematurely nor left hanging in an unresolved state.
For long requests that stream progress, set resetTimeoutOnProgress: true so each progress update resets the request timeout and a still-working, progressing request is not killed by the timeout.

Prioritize MCP validation and review effort by combining repository frequency with practitioner-confirmed severity and diagnostic effort: treat frequency counts as descriptive of the studied corpus rather than ecosystem prevalence, and remember that a rarely reported category (such as Authorization or other Security faults) can still be high severity while frequent categories cluster in Tool execution and data-schema enforcement.

Scope MCP audit conclusions to their validity boundaries: prevalence rates come from a public-server corpus (prototypes overrepresented), the proposed extensions are unvalidated testbed reference prototypes, and rates depend on the operational definitions used, so do not over-generalize them to proprietary or production systems.

When reviewing MCP state and configuration, check that server-level configuration parameters are actually enforced rather than accepted and silently ignored, that session identifiers are neither stale, reused, absent, nor stripped by middleware, and that server-managed resource state is persisted and kept fresh across operations.

When reviewing MCP resource handling, check resource identification (valid, resolvable resource URIs with the input URI format matching the internal normalized format) and resource synchronization (resources/updated notifications propagated so clients do not observe stale state).

When reviewing MCP prompt handling, check prompt identification (prompt lookup, correct handling of unknown prompt names, and error mapping to the appropriate MCP error code) and prompt argument handling (arguments conform to the declared input schema with correct types and value substitution).
When escalating an MCP issue, provide log excerpts, configuration files, reproduction steps, and environment details so it can be diagnosed.

When reviewing MCP model-provider integration, check model identification (valid model identifiers, supported sampling parameters, and models actually available through the configured provider) and provider integration (provider availability, complete initialization, and correct model listing during capability negotiation).

When reviewing MCP data and schema handling, check schema compatibility (emitted content conforms to the declared JSON Schema, with no missing required properties or format violations), data type and structure (schema-valid payloads whose values, such as permitted nulls, still violate downstream assumptions), and output representation (structured output conforms to the declared representation, not merely to valid JSON).

When reviewing MCP security, check authentication (Authorization header present, token well-formed and unexpired), token validation (token audience and other claims verified on receipt, tokens not forwarded upstream unverified), and authorization (access-control checks enforced after authentication before executing capabilities or tool invocations).

Validate the full MCP compliance surface — the initialize handshake, JSON-RPC 2.0 conformance, advertised capabilities (tools/prompts/resources), security, and registry/OSS conformance — rather than checking connectivity alone.

Build a fault taxonomy for an immature domain inductively: use faceted, bottom-up open coding rather than predefined categories, code artifacts independently with multiple coders and report inter-rater agreement, and iterate through refinement rounds until no new categories emerge (saturation).

Validate a fault taxonomy's external validity with an independent practitioner survey (respondents not involved in its construction) that captures, per subcategory, whether the fault was encountered in practice, its perceived severity, and its diagnostic effort, and treat the absence of newly reported categories as evidence of structural coverage.

Select information-rich cases by criterion-based purposive sampling when the goal is qualitative coverage of recurring fault patterns rather than statistical prevalence, and restrict mining to actively maintained engineered repositories using collaboration, activity, development-history, and popularity filters.
Require every vision tool schema to declare its coordinate convention and spatial semantics explicitly; undeclared coordinate conventions are a leading cause of silent misalignment.
Extend vision tool schemas with explicit semantic-role, modality, and coordinate-system fields; over 60% of composition failures came from schema-valid but semantically mismatched outputs.

Expect the recurring cross-case failure signature in deployed MCP vision toolchains: semantic misalignment despite valid schemas, fragmented spatial and temporal representations, and shallow wrappers unable to manage implicit state (evidenced across ParaView, SUMO+YOLO, ALITA, FHIR, and Blender case studies).

Attach runtime validator contracts that check spatial dimensions, tensor channel semantics, and coordinate alignment, and let agents halt, replan, or fall back on invariant violation; schema agreement alone does not prevent scale, modality, or layout failures.

Persist intermediate visual state in explicit, versioned, semantically namespaced memory with temporal scoping and provenance; undocumented or weak memory scoping is prevalent and produces stale-state warnings.

Bring all resizing, unit conversion, and schema coercion inside declared tool contracts; undocumented out-of-band bridging scripts (41% of deployments) break interpretability and trace-based recovery.

Select an MCP orchestration pattern by its trade-off and cover its dominant failure mode, and defer costly tool invocations when confidence is low or context is absent: static composition is auditable but brittle to drift, dynamic orchestration generalizes but needs runtime checks, multi-agent coordination parallelizes but risks memory leakage.

Establish protocol-level orchestration benchmarks and validator suites that emit binary results plus structured failure traces; without them, orchestration failures under injected errors go undetected and model benchmarks miss multi-tool correctness.

Build an MCP orchestration layer as a Mediator that is simultaneously an MCP server (exposing workflow tools to agents) and an MCP client (calling downstream MCP servers), so downstream servers stay unmodified and any MCP-compliant server is auto-discovered.

Constrain the orchestration DSL to a small fixed set of composable step primitives (call, loop, parallel, pipe, collect) and deliberately exclude conditionals, variables, and string manipulation, to keep semantics formal, failure modes predictable, and stop the DSL drifting into an accidental programming language.

For repeated, deterministic orchestration (the ~80% case), prefer a declarative blueprint over generated code because it gives sandboxing (only MCP tools are invocable), inspectability, design-time schema validation, and reliable LLM editability.
Do not deploy MCP into safety-critical domains before hardening the protocol layer with typed schemas, scoped memory, and introspectable execution traces.
