Keep mcp-scan security analysis enabled by default; use --skip-mcp-scan only when speed matters and security is out of scope, and ensure mcp-scan is installed (or explicitly disable the security validator) so runs do not silently lose security coverage.

Test a judge's discriminative validity with a label-flip perturbation: rewrite a response to invert its ground-truth label while preserving topic and structure; a reliable judge must flip its verdict.

Test a judge's consistency with meaning-preserving perturbations — formatting-only changes, semantic paraphrase, and verbosity variants — and require its score to stay constant when the underlying quality is unchanged.

Validate agentic judges separately from free-response judges — perturbing multi-turn transcripts both toward violations and toward compliance — because free-response reliability does not generalize to agentic settings and judges show asymmetric agentic failure modes (missing subtle violations versus over-flagging corrected transcripts).

Treat judge robustness as task-specific and re-validate a judge on each new task type rather than extrapolating its reliability from one task, since relative robustness rankings among judges can reverse across tasks and binary-stable judges can degrade badly on ordinal scoring.
Test for verbosity bias by holding factual content and intent constant while varying response length, to detect judges that over-reward longer answers or penalize more concise ones.

Measure stochastic stability by scoring duplicated identical inputs and treating any output variation as judge instability; fix or explicitly report the judge's sampling settings when stability matters.

For ordinal or graded scoring tasks, generate calibration samples targeting every score level (aim for an even distribution across the range) and report reliability with correlation and error metrics — Concordance Correlation Coefficient, Pearson's and Spearman's correlation, and Mean Absolute Error — not accuracy alone.

Select reliability test families by task type — label-flip plus binary invariance tests for binary classification, ordinal calibration plus invariance tests for graded scoring — rather than applying one fixed suite to every task.

When synthesizing graded test samples, use temperature ramping with a validator LLM that confirms the achieved label and retries at higher temperature on a miss, and guard diversity with a cosine-similarity check against both the few-shot examples and prior generations to prevent few-shot leakage.

Keep a human-in-the-loop review step to accept, edit, or reject generated perturbations and their labels, and expect to rely on it heavily when inducing rubric violations, because the generator model's own safety guardrails limit its ability to automatically degrade content into violations.
Control API cost and manual-review burden by down-sampling benchmarks with stratified sampling on category columns, so the subset stays representative of the original dataset.

Validate synthetic perturbations with a separate model before judging to confirm they hit their intended target labels, and configure a fallback validator for cases where the primary validator refuses on safety grounds.
Check a judge for inconsistency between its natural-language reasoning and its returned structured score, and substitute a different model for that judging task when such inconsistency appears.
Report per-test reliability (for example, per-benchmark, per-test heatmaps) rather than only an aggregate accuracy, because a single aggregate can hide large per-test variation.

Weight judge-reliability evidence by its strength: reliability results from small, down-sampled test sets (on the order of ten to sixteen samples) are preliminary and should be treated as directional rather than definitive.
Do not assume that naively ensembling several judges improves reliability; verify it empirically, since a three-judge ensemble did not exceed the best single judge in these experiments.

Gate every change to an MCP tool surface behind offline evaluation so regressions are caught before users see them and the change-feedback loop stays short; do not rely on a subjective 'it seems better' when deciding whether a change improved or regressed behaviour.

Because different LLMs use tools differently, evaluate each model-and-MCP pairing separately to measure compatibility, quality, and gaps rather than assuming results from one model transfer to another.

For benchmarks with a single tool call, model tool selection as multi-class classification (each tool is a class) and score it with accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 — accuracy over the whole dataset, and F1 as the harmonic mean summarizing precision and recall per tool.

Read the classification metrics diagnostically: low precision for a tool means it is being over-triggered (called when not expected), and low recall typically means it is under-triggered (missed, or confused with another tool); when two semantically similar tools are confused, expect the over-called tool's precision and the under-called tool's recall to both drop.

Treat benchmark volume as the limiting factor of offline evaluation: per-tool metrics built from only a couple of examples are not dependable, so grow per-tool benchmark coverage to make the classification metrics reliable.

Recognize that single-tool-call evaluation does not cover real sequential multi-tool flows, where later calls consume earlier outputs; to evaluate such flows, actually execute the tool calls or faithfully mock their responses instead of only fetching the tool list, and score selection as multi-label (not multi-class) classification when one input can trigger several tools.

Optimize tool provisioning for precision, not breadth: giving the model fewer, more relevant tools improves tool-calling accuracy (not merely token cost) by reducing decision complexity, letting the model spend reasoning on parameters and execution rather than tool disambiguation.

Evaluate a tool-selection system with retrieval metrics — Precision@K, Recall@K, F1@K, Hit Rate@K, MRR — and quantify savings with a Token Reduction Rate against the all-tools baseline, and interpret those metrics relative to catalog size (small catalogs inflate recall/F1 because more of the catalog is relevant).
Build a confusion matrix to see which tools are confused with each other, then use it to trace low precision or recall to specific tools and revise those tools' descriptions to reduce the confusion.

Score argument correctness with four targeted metrics — argument hallucination (arg names not defined for the tool), all-expected-arguments-provided, all-required-arguments-provided, and exact value match — and compute them only over tool calls that were correctly selected.
Provide searchable tool discovery with adjustable detail levels when filesystem browsing alone is not enough for efficient MCP tool selection.

As tool catalogs grow from hundreds toward thousands, intelligent tool discovery shifts from a nice-to-have optimization to a necessity, and is what makes large-scale multi-server MCP deployments economically feasible rather than prohibitive.
Avoid using the model context as a data bus for large intermediate results; move, filter, and summarize data inside the execution environment before returning model-visible output.

Read a `CallToolResult` as three separately-consumed fields — `content` for the model, `structured_content` (JSON matching the tool's output_schema) for application code, and `is_error` for success — and do not conflate the model-facing and code-facing halves.
Implement repeat checks, waits, retries, branching, and error handling in code rather than forcing every control-flow step through the model loop.
Keep intermediate and sensitive data outside the model context by default, and expose only explicitly logged, returned, or policy-approved values.
Use client-side tokenization or equivalent data-flow controls for sensitive fields that must pass between tools without being exposed to the model.

Apply least-exposure defaults for sensitive operations and data: offer a read-only mode for shared environments, demos, or observe-only use, and expose secret resources as metadata only (name, type, scope), never returning the secret value itself.
Persist intermediate state and reusable task code in the agent workspace when workflows need resume capability, progress tracking, or repeated execution.

Persist agent memory in an external store keyed by a session id (with a per-request invocation id) to give a stateless FaaS workflow multi-turn continuity; inject the retrieved memory into the planning stage, append only newly produced state each invocation, and reuse the store as a provenance and audit trail.
Run agent-generated code only inside a governed execution environment with sandboxing, resource limits, and monitoring.
Use deferred tool discovery for large tool libraries so the model loads only the tool definitions needed for the current task.
Configure deferred tool libraries with a small always-loaded core and a searchable long tail.

Treat context spent on tool definitions as a budget: keep it well under about 40% total utilization, accounting for other MCP servers whose definitions stack in the same client and for IDE/model tool caps (Cursor ~80, OpenAI 128, Claude ~120). This matters because models degrade at using information buried deep in a long context, so bloated tool metadata dilutes the signal available for the task.
Use programmatic tool calling for workflows where code can reduce context bloat, inference round-trips, or fragile manual synthesis.

Batch describe_tools: request schemas for all the tools you intend to use in a single call rather than one call per tool, to cut round-trips in a multi-tool workflow (which typically runs 6-8 tool calls versus 3 for a static toolset).
When enabling code-driven tool use, explicitly opt in only appropriate tools and keep their raw results inside the code-execution flow until the final output is ready.
Document programmatically called tools with clear return shapes so generated orchestration code can parse, aggregate, and compare outputs reliably.
Use tool input examples to teach conventions that schemas cannot express, including optional-field patterns, nested object usage, correlated parameters, and similar-tool disambiguation.
Write tool examples as concise realistic variants that show minimal, partial, and full calls only where they resolve real ambiguity.
Choose advanced tool-use features by diagnosing the active bottleneck before layering additional mechanisms.

Wrap and trim tool results to task-relevant fields: injecting the entire raw JSON response (metadata, headers, auxiliary fields) and retaining it across turns is a client orchestration-policy choice, not a protocol requirement, and is the dominant token inflator for off-the-shelf clients.

Reduce tool-schema injection cost: verbose JSON schemas loaded for every registered tool are the fixed planning overhead, so use deferred/lazy tool loading and trim schema verbosity rather than injecting the full tool list up front.

Treat session initialization and tool discovery as first-class measured cost: verbose schema serialization dominates initialization and is incurred before any user query, so log its token footprint and latency separately rather than amortizing it silently.

Treat per-turn MCP tool-schema injection as a first-class recurring cost (the Tools Tax): quantify it as approximately turns x catalog-size x ~200-500 tokens per tool, because stateless chat-completions APIs re-inject the full catalog on every turn and audits place it in the tens of thousands of tokens.

Load tool schemas in two phases: keep all compact tool summaries (target <=~60 tokens each) resident so the model stays aware the tools exist, and promote the full JSON schema on demand only for the gated top-k tools.

Prefer intent-gated two-phase loading over both naive full-schema injection and simple top-k retrieval of full schemas: it can cut measured per-turn tool tokens by roughly 95% while keeping effective context utilization high, and unlike static manual pruning it does not starve tasks of tools they need.

Expose the full JSON schema - not just the summary - for any tool the model will actually call, because the model needs full parameter specs to populate calls correctly; in ablation, dropping full-schema promotion was the single largest hit to task success.

Preserve JSON Schema 2020-12 (server): do not strip $schema, $defs, or additionalProperties, and keep composition (allOf/anyOf), conditional (if/then/else), and reference ($anchor) keywords intact through tools/list.

Profile both token cost and latency, and separate protocol token footprint (schemas, JSON tool calls, tool results tokenized under the same tokenizer) from LLM usage tokens, so cost is attributed to protocol representation versus model reasoning.

Optimize input-token consumption before FaaS execution, because LLM token charges dominate total cost (roughly 61-94%) and input-token volume drives both latency and cost, while agent and MCP function execution are comparatively negligible.

Prefer persistent HTTP/SSE transport over STDIO when initialization latency matters, because STDIO pays a per-connection cold-start penalty (spawning a subprocess); once connected, schema transfer is bandwidth-bound rather than compute-bound and negligible on either transport.

Treat model selection as a lever that reshapes both the cost profile and its predictability: small local models are fast on simple tool use but degrade with high latency variance on heavy-context, open-ended tasks, so favor models with stable, low-variance scaling where predictable latency matters.

Instrument the MCP workflow as a six-stage pipeline (S1 prompting, S2 planning, S3 tool call, S4 tool response, S5 context update, S6 answer synthesis) with a per-event structured log (identifiers, boundary timestamps and derived stage latency, model/tool/transport metadata, token accounting); when a client exposes no traces, reconstruct the stages from exported conversation logs.
Deliver logs to the client with log-message notifications on any transport, using MCP's eight RFC 5424 severity levels and honouring the client's runtime logging/setLevel choice.

Diagnose the bottleneck class from the client type before optimizing: customized environments suffer an input bottleneck determined by how fast the model parses tool definitions and plans, while off-the-shelf environments suffer an output bottleneck where unconstrained generation and streaming dominate user-perceived latency (final answer synthesis exceeds 75-86% of off-the-shelf-client latency).

Enforce profiling hygiene for stable, comparable stage attribution: disable response streaming and tool-execution caching, bound the agent horizon (rounds) and retries, and run tools sequentially; remember that black-box clients with provider-managed streaming fragment token delivery and can add latency unrelated to protocol communication.

Trust cross-model token comparisons despite differing tokenizers: per-query token counts across models correlate near-linearly (Pearson r >= 0.99), so the inexactness is a constant factor and relative rankings and latency trends hold; still normalize when reporting absolute counts.

Reducing orchestration overhead does not force a quality trade-off: on the benchmarks evaluated, protocol overhead and answer quality vary independently (85-100% accuracy maintained), so efficiency optimization can proceed without degrading task success.

Re-profile before assuming orchestration dominates in I/O-heavy production: because the six-stage decomposition isolates tool execution (S3-S4) from prompting, planning, and synthesis (S1-S2, S5-S6), it directly reveals the regime shift and quantifies orchestration overhead relative to tool latency when tools become heavy.

Account for measurement limitations before generalizing: post-hoc reconstruction of off-the-shelf clients from exported logs captures aggregate latency but misses millisecond jitter and silent internal retries, and single-hardware results may shift under different OS scheduling or STDIO buffering.

Default to retrieving K=3 tools as the operating point: it maximizes F1 (~58%) while holding a ~97% hit rate and ~0.91 MRR. Raising K above 3 adds little hit-rate/recall but sharply lowers precision; K=1 gives highest precision when a single tool suffices.

Treat tool-description quality as the retrieval ceiling: invest in informative, semantically distinct descriptions. Poorly documented tools are under-retrieved regardless of embedding model, and servers with overlapping descriptions (e.g. read/write/copy/move file) suffer lower MRR, while distinct domain vocabulary retrieves near-perfectly at low K.

When tools are semantically overlapping, add discriminating signals beyond description embeddings — parameter-level matching or tool-usage-frequency — to break ties, since embedding similarity alone surfaces related-but-wrong tools among near-duplicates.

Route tools by Intent-Schema Overlap - cosine similarity between the query embedding and a compact tool-summary embedding - and admit a tool only when it clears a threshold; ISO is a cheap embedding-space proxy for the attention a tool would actually receive, so a low-ISO tool can be dropped without changing the decision.

Construct each tool's embedding document from a structured template (name, purpose, expanded capabilities, parameter descriptions) so the matcher has multiple semantic anchors for user intent, rather than embedding a bare tool name or one-line description.

For ambiguous queries that lack domain specificity, do not just return the raw top-K: fold conversational context (prior tool use, active server sessions) into the query embedding, or prompt the user to clarify before retrieving, to avoid a mixed cross-domain tool set.

For cross-domain queries that need tools from multiple servers, decompose the intent into sub-tasks and retrieve tools per sub-task (multi-query retrieval); a single top-K retrieval often surfaces only one domain and misses the others.

Design a graceful-degradation fallback so the LLM always receives a minimal tool context: when no tool clears the similarity threshold, return the top-K anyway, or fall back to the all-tools baseline for low-confidence queries, or route to a human operator.

Treat the tool index as live infrastructure: new tools must be embedded and indexed before they are discoverable (~2s per tool), and fast-changing catalogs need a scheduled re-indexing pipeline that refreshes embeddings whenever tool descriptions change.

Instrument a feedback loop that records which tools were actually invoked, task success or failure, and user feedback, and use that signal to refine embeddings and tune retrieval parameters over time.
For high-throughput deployments with recurring query patterns, cache the retrieved tool set for common patterns to cut retrieval latency further, on top of the already sub-100ms search.

Keep the retrieval architecture modular with independently replaceable embedding models, vector stores, and retrieval parameters so it adapts as the MCP ecosystem and embedding technology evolve. A proven default instantiation is a vector database such as Milvus, a general-purpose text embedding model, dot-product similarity, and the official MCP SDK — treated as swappable defaults, not requirements.

Do not treat the reported parameters or accuracy figures as universal: they come from a single embedding model (text-embedding-ada-002), a single LLM (GPT-4o), single-turn offline evaluation, and at most 121 tools. Re-validate K, model choice, and multi-turn and at-scale behaviour in your own deployment before relying on them.

Flag when the tool catalog is large enough that the Tools Tax dominates the effective context window; reasoning quality degrades sharply once effective context utilization exceeds roughly 70%, so the tax erodes usable reasoning surface, not just budget.

Gate the active tool set on both semantic relevance and authoritative state: admit a tool only if ISO meets the threshold AND the agent state satisfies its preconditions, then take the top-k; state preconditions are deterministic and cannot be bypassed by an adversarial paraphrase the way free-text matching can.

Add a deterministic hallucination-rejection gate: if the model calls a tool whose full schema was not promoted this turn, reject the call with a structured error listing the available tools; this downstream catch is what makes aggressive gating safe by turning routing false-negatives into recoverable events.

Default to a small sentence encoder (e.g. all-MiniLM-L6-v2, 384-d) for tool routing: routing is sub-millisecond and cheap, larger encoders add only marginal recall at multiples of the latency, and the hallucination gate absorbs the occasional routing miss.

Calibrate the routing threshold per deployment against a held-out set of query/ground-truth-tool pairs by maximizing F1 (values around 0.22-0.32 are typical), and set top-k conservatively large (~8-12), relying on the threshold rather than a tight k for precision.

Design the prompt layout for cache reuse: keep the stable summary pool in the prompt prefix so it earns prompt-cache credit, and place the per-turn promoted schemas immediately before the user message to minimize cache invalidation.

Emit a structured observability event for every routing decision (candidate scores, state-gated-out set, active set, phase-1 and phase-2 token counts, latency) so routing can be audited for misfires and fed into cost dashboards.

Keep measured and projected results strictly separate and never let a projection inherit the confidence of a measurement: report directly measured quantities (token counts, context-utilization ratios) distinctly from downstream figures extrapolated from them (success, latency, cost, quality), and mark the extrapolations as such.

Keep preconditions and the hallucination gate as components in their own right, not just the semantic router: each independently contributes measurable task success in ablation, and together they make aggressive routing recoverable and deterministic.

Use semantic (embedding) matching rather than lexical/TF-IDF matching for tool routing: lexical matching materially lowers task success, while a larger embedding model barely helps - the value is in semantics, not encoder size.

Tune k and the ISO threshold toward recall unless the token budget is the binding constraint: raising the threshold or shrinking k saves tokens but costs task success, and the highest-k settings buy little extra success for many more tokens.

Size the mitigation to catalog growth: under naive injection the tax crosses the ~70% utilization fracture point around 50 tools, whereas gating holds utilization near-flat into the thousands - treat roughly 50 tools as the point where eager schema injection becomes untenable.

Treat gating as a security by-product, not a security guarantee: excluding tools whose summaries do not match intent shrinks the tool-poisoning attack surface, but an adversarial paraphrase can still be gated in, so pair gating with a runtime attention-energy or anomaly monitor for genuine defense.

Position application-layer tool gating as a deploy-today mitigation that composes with - but does not replace - protocol-level fixes (e.g. transport-layer schema caching) and output-side optimizations (e.g. code-execution patterns); intent gating with preconditions remains necessary even after transport caching arrives.

When implementing the router, over-fetch a candidate slate wider than k before applying threshold and precondition filters, cache promoted schemas in an LRU keyed by tool id, and normalize embeddings so an inner-product index computes cosine similarity directly.

Optimize for effective context utilization (context engineering), not raw context-window length: protocol-level efficiency is the binding constraint on scalable agentic systems, so a longer context window does not remove the need to gate tool context.

For multi-hop workflows where the right tool only becomes relevant after an intermediate result, re-embed the query after each observation to refresh routing rather than routing solely on the first user message; this is a known, if still preliminary, improvement for long-horizon tasks.

When an LLM agent performs a recurring multi-step tool task, separate one-time intelligence (deciding what to do) from repeated execution (carrying it out): have the agent reason once to produce a reusable plan, then execute that plan with no further agent reasoning.

Structure the agent lifecycle into a one-time design phase (explore downstream tools via tools/list and trial calls, then build a blueprint) and a repeated execution phase triggered by a single call that runs with zero agent involvement.

When a task cannot be fully automated, use a hybrid pattern: have the engine execute the mechanical parts in a loop and return a single batch (collect) for the agent to reason over, giving O(1) agent reasoning passes instead of O(N).
In the tool-executing agent, gate the tool-call node behind a conditional edge so tools run only when the LLM actually requests them, and cap the tool loop (LangGraph defaults to 25 supersteps).

Prefer persisting full agent memory (internal reasoning plus tool inputs and outputs) over naively replaying cumulative client request/response history, because client-only memory repeats already-completed work while agent memory lets the planner skip failed strategies and the actor skip redundant tool calls.

Do not assume an agent will use memory just because it was injected: LLMs often ignore available context and repeat tool calls, so add an explicit system-prompt instruction telling the agent to check prior tool responses and reuse that data before making new calls.

Capture the agent's plan as a declarative JSON blueprint that is parameterized (runtime values via {{params.*}} templates), portable (version in Git, share, schedule via cron), and inspectable (human- and machine-readable for validation and audit).

Give each agent a strict-JSON prompt contract - the planner returns the tools and their sequence, the actor executes them in order, and the evaluator returns success, needs_retry, reason, and feedback - so every agent's output can be parsed deterministically by downstream agents and branching logic.

Flow data implicitly between steps through a resolver context that stores each step's output at steps.<id>, and when a value is a single template expression return the raw resolved object (not a stringified form) for type-safe piping, rather than using explicit variables.

Give each workflow an explicit error strategy (abort for critical pipelines, continue for best-effort sync, or retry-with-backoff for transient failures), accumulate errors for partial-success runs, and validate blueprint structure at design time (block on structural errors, warn on unknown tools).
Make repeated or scheduled writes idempotent (for example, use upsert/MERGE semantics) so re-runs converge to the same state and add or update resources without creating duplicates.

Reuse the dual-role Mediator beyond workflow execution (aggregation, caching, audit, rate-limiting, all without modifying downstream servers), and apply the design-once/trigger-many pattern to any domain with repeated multi-step tool orchestration.

Host MCP-enabled agentic workflows on serverless FaaS rather than monolithic VMs to gain autoscaling and pay-per-request cost efficiency, but design every component around FaaS statelessness from the outset.

Decompose the agentic pattern into one FaaS function per role (e.g. Planner, Actor, Evaluator) orchestrated as a FaaS workflow, so no single function risks the platform timeout and each role can be scaled and configured independently while sharing stateless instances.

Automate MCP-server-to-FaaS packaging by parsing the server source (AST) to detect tool functions and generating the request handler, telemetry, caching, and container deployment, instead of hand-writing per-server glue.

Provision MCP servers cost-consciously by choosing among independent, per-workflow-unified, or globally-unified (colocated) deployment, because FaaS bills on peak memory and execution time; colocating shared or remote servers near their workflows cuts latency and management overhead.

Consolidate an application's MCP servers into a single FaaS function (memory set to the peak of the constituents) to reduce cold-start overhead and stabilize latency, accepting a higher per-invocation cost; keep singleton per-server deployment when minimizing per-function memory footprint matters more.
Model each agent as a graph (e.g. LangGraph) but externalize its state as explicit inter-function messages, because in-memory graph state does not survive a single function invocation.

Structure the reasoning loop as a bounded cycle: the Evaluator returns success to the user or routes structured feedback back to the Planner for a revised plan, and the loop must terminate at an explicit maximum-iteration cap.
Bound the agent loop with an explicit maximum-iteration cap and require the evaluator to emit feedback on retry that the planner consumes to revise its plan.

Inject only the relevant slice of memory into the context rather than everything, because stale or off-topic memory distracts the LLM and inflates latency and cost; curate what state is supplied and optionally summarize or knowledge-graph-distill it before storage.

Value persisted memory and caching for reliability, not only efficiency: they raised completion rates (eliminating the failures seen in memoryless runs) and mitigated the impact of LLM non-determinism and temperature on practical workflows.

Keep large content and file artifacts out of the LLM context and off the function's local disk: store them in object storage (S3) and pass URLs, because oversized inline outputs overwhelm the context window and stateless FaaS does not persist local files across invocations.

Cache deterministic MCP tool outputs, keyed by a hash of tool name plus parameters and stored in object storage with a per-tool TTL, so repeated identical calls in a session return a cached handle instead of re-executing the tool.
MCP invocation caching pays off only after a warmup call and works by returning a stored object handle instead of full content, cutting both repeated MCP execution latency and input tokens.

When an MCP server must expose many tools (dozens to hundreds), do not load every tool definition statically; use a dynamic/lazy discovery mechanism, because static exposure grows token usage roughly linearly with toolset size and soon hits the context-window limit.

Agent memory combined with MCP caching beats memoryless baselines across latency, tokens, and cost (up to 13x, 88%, and 66% respectively), and the empty-memory configuration fails follow-up queries that lack earlier context.

Choose an orchestration framework that models the workflow as an explicit graph over shared, persisted state (e.g. LangGraph) when you need developer control over branching, conditional routing, and retries, rather than a framework that prescribes a fixed reasoning strategy.

Prefer CLI over MCP when the agent already knows the tool from training data (e.g. gh, kubectl, terraform) or when a single piped command composes several operations in one call: the agent pays zero schema overhead, gets terse predictable output, and avoids per-step LLM round-trips. A short (~800-token) skills document can further cut CLI tool calls and latency.

Prefer MCP over CLI when the platform's API surface is larger than the agent's training knowledge (use a describe/discovery tool for runtime capability discovery instead of guessing undocumented calls), in multi-tenant or multi-user environments (per-user OAuth, explicit tool boundaries, structured audit trails instead of ambient credentials), or when safety requires constraining the agent to declared tools with typed inputs rather than arbitrary shell.

Encode operational knowledge the agent cannot infer into the instruction/skill layer: the platform scoping hierarchy (e.g. account -> org -> project), strict dependency ordering (verify referenced resources exist before creating dependents), and phase-gated workflows with explicit 'do not proceed until this step is done' checkpoints, so the agent orders operations correctly on the first attempt instead of discovering dependencies through failures.
Maintain one canonical definition per agent command/skill and symlink it into each IDE's command directory (Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf) so a single source of truth propagates everywhere on update.

Require explicit human-in-the-loop confirmation for all write operations (e.g. via MCP elicitation: the agent states its intent, the user approves or rejects) and make destructive operations fail closed, blocking delete entirely when the client cannot support a confirmation flow, so there are no silent mutations or deletions.

Add operational guardrails for a resource-mutating agent: configurable rate limits (e.g. a sane default like 10 req/s), automatic retries with backoff for transient failures, and bounded pagination to prevent runaway list operations.

Offer two transports so the server scales from local to team use: a stdio transport for zero-configuration local IDE integration, and a session-based streamable-HTTP transport for remote/team deployment with sessions reaped on a timeout, CORS restricted, and per-IP rate limits.

Reduce the context and configuration the developer must supply: let every tool accept an optional URL parameter and auto-extract scope identifiers (account, org, project, resource) from a pasted platform URL, and support startup-time toolset filtering so the agent only sees resource types for the modules a team actually uses.
Support tag or namespace filters (for example source:hubspot or hubspot/deals) in tool search so the LLM can narrow results precisely instead of relying on semantic ranking alone.

Budget for the dynamic-toolset trade-off: expect about 2-3x more tool calls and roughly 50% higher execution time than a static toolset; net total tokens and runtime still do not rise because input tokens fall by more than 96%.

For token-critical or large MCP servers, prefer dynamic toolsets: they hold token consumption roughly constant from 40 to 400 tools and cut total tokens by about 90-96% at a 100% task success rate, and adding new tools does not raise baseline token usage.
If tool-call count (steps/latency) matters more than token cost, collapse search_tools and describe_tools into a single call, accepting higher token usage as the deliberate trade-off.

When choosing between dynamic toolsets and a bespoke 'code mode' runtime, weigh that code mode can sidestep context limits entirely but demands significant engineering investment and domain expertise most teams lack; dynamic toolsets on standard MCP are the lower-investment path.

Exploit the conversation history as a cache: once a tool's description and schema are loaded, reuse them in later steps instead of issuing fresh search/describe calls - this is what makes overhead shrink for longer-running agents.

Remember that category-based discoverability depends on the quality of the source OpenAPI or function documentation; treat semantic search as the fallback that does not depend on that documentation quality.

Do not take vendor token-reduction and success-rate figures at face value: validate them against your own model and task mix, because the headline results were measured with Claude Sonnet 4.5 and a specific success definition (calling the expected tools with the expected arguments).

Understand the client-mode harness contract: the framework starts a test server for the scenario, appends the server URL as the client's final argument, sets MCP_CONFORMANCE_SCENARIO (and MCP_CONFORMANCE_CONTEXT with scenario data such as credentials), then captures and checks the protocol interactions.
In server mode the server under test must already be running and the SDK owns its full lifecycle (start, health-check, cleanup) while the harness connects as an MCP client.

A client under test must derive its lifecycle from the protocol version it is told to run — stateful (initialize handshake) for dated versions through 2025-11-25, stateless (per-request _meta) for the 2026 draft — and use the forwarded MCP_CONFORMANCE_PROTOCOL_VERSION.

Request metadata (client): send MCP-Protocol-Version on every POST, populate the three required _meta fields on every request, keep the header equal to _meta.protocolVersion, and retry with a supported version when the first is rejected.

Let the Client negotiate the protocol version (it probes the server and falls back to the classic handshake for older servers) rather than pinning a version, unless you have a specific reason to control it.
Treat an out-of-applicability spec version as a skip: a scenario requested outside its applicability window exits 0 (skipped) unless --force is passed.

Use an expected-failures baseline to keep CI green on known failures while still catching regressions, remembering it is bidirectional: a newly failing unlisted scenario and a now-passing still-listed scenario both exit 1 (the latter is a stale entry to remove).
Prefer the shipped composite GitHub Action over hand-rolled conformance scripts, and in server mode start and health-check your own server before invoking it.

Use the sdk subcommand as the cross-SDK inner loop (it clones, builds, and runs the local conformance build against a ref) and pass --mode client or --mode server, since each side is tested and scored independently.

Model an SDK's example conformance server on the reference everything-server: implement the full feature surface (tools, resources, prompts, all log levels, completion, list-changed, subscribe/update), use the standardized names (test_ prefix for tools/prompts, test:// for resources), and reproduce its automatic behaviors (dynamic registration about 2s after start, watched-resource update about every 3s) so one suite verifies every SDK.

SDK build/run commands come from the built-in KNOWN_SDKS table (no repo config needed) and any field is overridable on the CLI (CLI flag beats built-in), so override per-ref rather than editing the table for a one-off.
Assess an SDK's tier with the tier-check subcommand against SEP-1730.

Every check should carry specReferences to the governing spec section, and its severity must follow the spec keyword — MUST/MUST NOT to FAILURE, SHOULD/SHOULD NOT to WARNING — noting CI treats WARNING as failing, so Tier-1 SDKs must satisfy SHOULDs too.

Read the traceability manifest correctly: it is generated from a real reference-SDK run (so dynamic check IDs resolve), tested means the check ID was emitted (not that any SDK passes — that is tier-check), and a SEP absent from it has no conformance artifacts and is not-started.
Relegation (SEP-1730): an SDK drops from Tier 1 to Tier 2 if any conformance test fails continuously for 4 weeks, and from Tier 2 to Tier 3 if more than 20% fail continuously for 4 weeks.
Add a scenario by implementing the Scenario interface (start/stop/getChecks) under src/scenarios/<name>/ and registering it in src/scenarios/index.ts.
Optimize for spec coverage, not harness polish: the coverage that matters is how much of the protocol the scenarios exercise.
Follow the repo toolchain conventions: use npm (never commit pnpm or yarn lockfiles) and open an issue to align before a scenario or bug-fix PR.

Do not point an agent at the repo to find bugs generically; give it a concrete target (a specific unmet spec MUST/SHOULD or an open issue), because generic bug-hunting on a test harness yields low-signal PRs.

Prefer one scenario with many checks over many single-check scenarios — the strongest scenario-design rule — because per-scenario HTTP-server overhead multiplies across every SDK's CI, there is less to maintain, and pass-N/M-checks is finer signal.

Apply the granularity heuristic — would someone implement a server/client that does just this? — merging scenarios that would always be built together and keeping them separate only when genuinely independent or mutually exclusive.
When a PR adds scenarios, start with one end-to-end happy-path scenario carrying many checks; never split it into step-1 and step-1+2 scenarios, since the larger subsumes the smaller.

Give a check one slug shared by its SUCCESS and FAILURE outcomes (flip status and errorMessage), optimize the code for Ctrl+F on that slug (repetition beats a clever helper), and reuse ConformanceCheck and other shared types rather than parallel shapes.

Do not reimplement the runner: a new subcommand that selects, runs, summarizes, and exit-codes scenarios must go through the existing client/server commands (subprocess) or shared helpers, never a parallel suite or summary loop.

Never report a missing prerequisite as SKIPPED: because SKIPPED counts as green in pass counts, exit codes, and baselines, a check that cannot be exercised (missing fixture, rejected probe, undeclared feature) must FAIL via notTestable()/untestableCheck() naming the missing prerequisite; reserve SKIPPED for genuinely inapplicable checks.
Be precise about required versus optional in scenario prose — never promote a MAY or SHOULD to a MUST — and consult the actual modelcontextprotocol spec, not guesses, for spec details.
Take a SEP's requirement levels from its spec diff (the docs/specification/draft/ change), not the SEP summary or PR description, since the governing keyword lives in the spec text.

Review against the spec diff as ground truth: read the RFC-2119 sentences yourself rather than trusting the PR description or SEP summary, and treat a SEP's conformance-test-case table as authoritative for its cases, flagging a table/prose mismatch as a spec gap rather than silently resolving it.

Ship every new scenario with both a passing example (extend the everything-client/server) and a negative test that asserts the specific FAILURE/WARNING, because a green run only proves no false-positive, not that the check catches anything.

Demand proof it runs and a real negative test: the PR must cite a real implementation it ran green against (the everything-server or an external SDK via the pkg.pr.new preview), and its negative test must pin the specific failing check slugs rather than merely assert the failure count is greater than zero.

Before opening a PR, ensure npm run build and npm test pass, run non-trivial scenario changes against a real SDK (typescript or python), and exercise shared-infrastructure changes (runner, tier-check) against go or csharp too.

Know the output contract: results land in results/<scenario>-<timestamp>/ (server mode results/server-<scenario>-<timestamp>/), and each result is a ConformanceCheck (id, name, description, status, timestamp, specReferences, details) in checks.json.

Emit a structured, timestamped aggregated report: one JSON report per server (named <server>.json under output/), an aggregate servers_validation.json, and a Markdown summary table of per-server status/errors/warnings — recording Name, Command, Status, counts, and report file, and adding an Error_Message on failures.

CLI arguments are Zod-validated before the runner runs (client: non-empty command, existing scenario, positive-integer timeout; server: valid HTTP/HTTPS URL, existing scenarios, default to all), so rely on that validation rather than re-checking.

Import protocol types from the vendored spec-types/<version> copies (not @modelcontextprotocol/sdk) so scenarios can target draft versions before any SDK implements them, and never hand-edit those files — refresh via npm run sync-schema and let SOURCE record the commit.

Import the schema version a scenario or connection actually uses: a scenario imports the version matching its source.introducedIn, and a Connection imports the version whose lifecycle it implements (stateful to 2025-11-25, stateless to draft).
Serve conformance over Streamable HTTP and catch/handle notification promise rejections when no client is connected, so stray notification errors do not crash the server.

Protect localhost servers against DNS rebinding in production using createMcpExpressApp() or the localhostHostValidation() middleware (validate Host/Origin, reject non-localhost); the no-dns-rebinding-protection example exists only as a negative test expected to FAIL and must never be a production pattern.

OAuth client authorization-server binding: on a Protected-Resource-Metadata flip to a new authorization server (a new issuer surfacing on a 401), the client MUST re-register with the new AS rather than reuse the old credentials.
OAuth client resource validation: per RFC 8707 a client MUST verify the PRM resource matches the server URL it is accessing and abort authorization on a mismatch.

OAuth client scopes and registration: with offline_access in the AS scopes_supported a client SHOULD include refresh_token in grant_types (and MAY include offline_access in the request scope); when the server lacks DCR it MUST use pre-registered credentials via context; it should follow the WWW-Authenticate scope from the 401; and it validates the iss parameter when the server advertises it.
Elicitation client: apply default values for omitted fields (string, integer, number, enum, boolean) before returning an elicitation response.

Elicitation (server): include default values in the elicitation schema across string, integer, number, enum, and boolean fields, and encode enum schemas by shape (untitled single-select as an enum array, titled single-select as oneOf with const/title, the legacy titled form as the deprecated enumNames, untitled multi-select as items.enum, titled multi-select as items.anyOf).
MCP request headers (client): on Streamable HTTP POSTs send Mcp-Method (mirroring the JSON-RPC method) and Mcp-Name (mirroring params.name or params.uri for tools/call, resources/read, prompts/get).

MCP request-header validation (server, SEP-2243): reject a request whose Mcp-Method or Mcp-Name header disagrees with the body (or is missing for a name-carrying body) with HTTP 400 and JSON-RPC -32020 (HeaderMismatch); treat header names case-insensitively but values case-sensitively, accept optional whitespace around Mcp-Name per RFC 9110 section 5.5, and reject a request where a custom header is omitted while its value is present in the body.

Select the Client transport by the type of its single positional argument: an MCPServer/Server instance for in-process, a URL string for Streamable HTTP, or a transport object (usable as `async with ... as (read, write)`) for anything else.

x-mcp-header extension (client): mirror each annotated parameter into an Mcp-Param-{Name} header (plain ASCII direct, Base64 for non-ASCII/whitespace/control), add no Mcp-Param header for unannotated params, omit it when the value is null or absent, and reject invalid annotations (empty, non-primitive, duplicate including case-insensitive, or containing space/colon/non-ASCII/control).

JSON Schema $ref safety: never automatically dereference a $ref that resolves to a network URI (only same-document JSON Pointers and internal $anchor are safe), because a network $ref is an SSRF and fetch-DoS vector.

Multi-Round Tool Resolution (client): echo requestState unchanged on retry, include none when the server sent none, use a new JSON-RPC id per retry, treat a missing resultType as complete, and never leak inputResponses or requestState into other requests.

SSE retry (client): respect the retry field (wait the given milliseconds), treat a graceful stream closure as reconnectable (reconnect via GET), and send Last-Event-ID on reconnection for resumability.

InputRequiredResult (server): respond with InputRequiredResult (inputRequests and/or requestState) to gather input; always include resultType, never return it on unsupported methods, reject tampered requestState, include inputRequests only for declared client capabilities, and return JSON-RPC errors for protocol-level input errors.

Stateless requests (server, SEP-2575): carry the request JSON-RPC id on every error, and reject a request with missing _meta — or _meta lacking io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion, clientInfo, or clientCapabilities — with -32602.
Latch check results by severity: a single non-conformant request is a violation even if later ones conform, so never let a later better status overwrite a worse one for the same request id.

Caching hints (server): include ttlMs and cacheScope on cacheable results (tools/list, prompts/list, resources/list, resources/templates/list, resources/read), with non-negative-integer ttlMs and a cacheScope of public or private.
Lifecycle (server): respond to initialize with a valid structure and make any server-provided session ID visible-ASCII only.
Resource errors (server): for a non-existent resource return -32602 (Invalid Params) rather than an empty contents array, and include the requested URI in the error data.
Concurrent SSE (server): give each POST request its own SSE stream with a unique stream ID, and keep the standalone GET stream (without Last-Event-ID) limited to one per session.

SSE polling and resumption (server): send a priming event (id plus empty data) and a retry field on POST SSE streams, and support closing a stream mid-operation then replaying events on reconnect with Last-Event-ID including via GET.
Tool naming (server): a tool name must be 1 to 64 characters and match ^[A-Za-z0-9_./-]+$.
Tasks capability (SEP-2663): advertise the io.modelcontextprotocol/tasks extension, gate the v2 task surface on capability negotiation, and support SEP-2575 per-request capability overrides.

Tasks dispatch (SEP-2663): reject the removed v1 methods tasks/result and tasks/list with -32601; allow server-directed task creation without a client task hint (tolerating and ignoring the legacy task param on sync tools); let a fast operation return a sync ToolResult; stamp every non-task response with the resultType 'complete' discriminator; and guarantee strong consistency, where tasks/get right after a CreateTaskResult resolves and an unknown taskId returns -32602.

Tasks required-capability (SEP-2575/2663): if a required-task tool is called by a client that did not declare the tasks extension at initialize, reject with -32021 (MissingRequiredClientCapability) and put a requiredCapabilities object (mirroring InitializeRequest) in the error data so the client can self-describe.

Tasks wire hygiene (SEP-2663): the tasks-v2 wire defines no requestState (keep it off CreateTaskResult and DetailedTask), uses the renamed ttlMs and pollIntervalMs fields, enforces no-early-TTL-expiry, and drops the redundant v1 related-task _meta key because the taskId is already at root.

Tasks and MRTR composition (SEP-2663): when a tool gathers input via the MRTR loop then escalates to async, the inlined CreateTaskResult must reflect the MRTR-gathered answer — wiring MRTR and tasks as independent surfaces fails the end-to-end check.

The tasks status-notifications scenario is a known harness gap left SKIPPED: SEP-2663 emits notifications/tasks over the SEP-2575 subscriptions/listen stream, which this tools/call-POST-observing harness never opens, so do not read its SKIP as a server defect.
Authorization-server metadata: a conformant AS metadata response must set client_id_metadata_document_supported to true to signal Client ID Metadata Document (CIMD) support.
Tier thresholds (SEP-1730): Tier 1 requires a 100% conformance pass rate, Tier 2 at least 80%, and Tier 3 no minimum, where the pass rate is passed/(passed+failed)*100 over date-versioned scenarios.

Tier definitions (SEP-1730): an issue is triaged at its first label (labeling and validity, not resolution), and a P0 is a CVSS>=7.0 security vulnerability or a core-functionality failure blocking connection, message exchange, or use of core primitives.

Tier responsiveness commitments (SEP-1730): new-feature support before each spec release (Tier 1) versus within 6 months (Tier 2); issue triage within 2 business days versus within 30 days; P0 resolution within 7 days versus within 14.

Tier release, docs, and policy obligations (SEP-1730): Tier 1 needs a stable release >=1.0.0 with no pre-release plus a documented breaking-change policy, all-feature docs with examples, a published dependency policy, and a concrete roadmap; Tier 2 needs at least one stable release, core-feature docs, a dependency policy, and a plan toward Tier 1.

Tier 1 gate — require ALL of: server and client conformance at 100% (date-versioned), triage compliance >=90% within 2 business days, all P0s resolved within 7 days, a stable release >=1.0.0 with no pre-release, a documented breaking-change policy, all non-experimental features documented with examples, a published dependency policy, and a concrete roadmap.

Tier 2 gate — require ALL of: server and client conformance >=80% (date-versioned), triage compliance >=80% within 1 month, P0s resolved within 2 weeks, at least one stable release >=1.0.0, core-feature docs, a published dependency policy, and a plan toward Tier 1; otherwise the SDK is Tier 3.

Scoring scope: only date-versioned scenarios count toward tier while draft and extension scenarios are informational, and the --spec-version flag filters date versions cumulatively but matches draft and extension exactly.
Issue-label taxonomy: apply the consistent 12 labels (3 type, 5 status, 4 priority) to enable automated tier reporting.

Pre-flight a tier audit: verify gh auth status and conformance-server reachability first and stop with a clear message if either fails, since the everything server must be running for server conformance to be measured.
Always pass tier-check --branch (derived from the local checkout when not given) so policy signal-file checks run against the correct branch rather than the repo default.

Split the audit correctly: the deterministic tier-check CLI computes conformance (both sides, per version), triage, P0, labels, release, policy signals, and spec tracking into JSON, while AI evaluations judge only documentation coverage and policy substance, reading only the files the CLI already found.
When no client conformance command exists, skip client conformance and note it as a gap, but do not block tier advancement on that skip alone.
Interpret pass rates through the expected-failures baseline: a low rate from unimplemented OAuth scenarios (a scope gap) differs sharply from one from broken core functionality.

Present conformance as one server-plus-client matrix, deriving the client category from the scenario name (an auth/ prefix means Auth, everything else Core, and all server scenarios are Core); failures clustered in Client: Auth at the newest version read as a scope gap (new auth features not yet implemented), while failures in Server or Client: Core are more concerning.

Audit P0 labels: a high P0 count (more than 2) alongside otherwise strong Tier-2 metrics signals mislabeling (enhancements filed as P0), so recommend a P0 label audit rather than hard-blocking on the count.

Understand the traceability YAML's job (SEP-2484): map each spec-diff normative sentence to a check: ID (testable) or an excluded: reason (not testable); the CLI scaffolds the skeleton and you fill the rows from the diff, and the SEP number is the source PR number.
When a requirement is ambiguous, leave a TODO: row rather than guess, because humans review the traceability yaml before scenarios are written.
Diff the traceability YAML against the spec sentences and flag any row that paraphrases rather than quotes, claims a keyword level the spec does not support, or asserts something the spec never says.
Extract requirements by quoting the whole normative sentence (a lead-in MUST/SHOULD is inherited by its bullets) and reading context, because regex matching alone is insufficient (issue #243).

Map RFC 2119 severity to YAML: MUST, MUST NOT, SHALL, SHALL NOT, and REQUIRED become a check: row at FAILURE; SHOULD and SHOULD NOT become a check: row at WARNING; MAY and OPTIONAL produce no row at all.

Follow traceability YAML conventions: use the same id for SUCCESS and FAILURE, lowercase-kebab slugs from the verb phrase, check: rows leading with check: (then text, then optional url), excluded: rows leading with text: (then excluded, then optional issue), and all check: rows before all excluded: rows, separated by one blank line and never interleaved.

Gate exclusions: mark a requirement excluded: only when the harness cannot protocol-observe it, and never on your own authority — get user sign-off, batching clearly-excluded rows in one question and asking borderline rows (internal-state, UI/human-facing, or precondition phrasing) one per row.
Resolve a traceability row's spec reference as row.url falling back to file.spec_url, so a requirement from a different spec page carries a full url: override.

Before proposing a new scenario file, look for an existing host to fold the checks into (fewer scenarios, more checks): derive the suite from the requirement subject (clients to client/, servers to server/, authorization servers to authorization-server/), search it for scenarios on the same spec area, and recommend a host by path or state explicitly that none fits.

Test spec backing: a check is legitimate only if a fully compliant implementation would not fail it; if a compliant implementation would fail, or two compliant SDKs in different languages diverge, the behavior is unpinned — flag it as a spec gap rather than enforce it.

Hunt for dead checks (a FAILURE with no reachable SUCCESS counterpart, or an always-false guard) and weak logic (a missing or malformed input that silently passes, or an assertion that cannot distinguish rejected-for-the-right-reason from rejected-at-all).

Structure review output: order findings spec-backing, then logic/dead, then coverage, then conventions; make each a self-contained bullet carrying the check id, a head-SHA-pinned file:line permalink, the quoted normative sentence, and the consequence; and keep spec gaps in a separate trailing list because they go upstream, not to the PR author.
Launch the MCP Inspector with `npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector <command>`; no installation step is required.

Match the Inspector launch wrapper to how the server is distributed: `npx <pkg>` for an npm package, `uvx <pkg>` for a PyPI package, `node <entry>.js` for a local TypeScript server, and `uv --directory <path> run <pkg>` for a local Python server.

Launch the Inspector via npx without cloning its repository (Node.js ^22.7.5 required): pass server arguments directly, set the server's environment variables with -e, and separate inspector flags from server arguments with `--`.
Read a server's README for its exact startup command and arguments before inspecting it.
Use the server connection pane to select the transport and, for local servers, set the command-line arguments and environment before connecting.

Connect the server end via mcpServer.connect(serverTransport) with the high-level McpServer (which delegates to this.server.connect); with the low-level Server class, call server.connect(serverTransport) directly.

Exercise each capability surface through its tab rather than only checking connectivity: Resources (metadata, content, subscriptions), Prompts (custom arguments and previewed output), and Tools (custom inputs and observed results).
Begin every Inspector session by verifying basic connectivity and confirming capability negotiation before deeper testing.
Watch the Notifications pane for the server's logs and notifications when diagnosing its behaviour.
After changing server code, rebuild the server and reconnect the Inspector before re-testing — it does not pick up changes live — then test the affected features while monitoring messages.
Deliberately test edge cases — invalid inputs, missing prompt arguments, concurrent operations — and verify the server returns proper error responses.

Treat the MCP Inspector as two cooperating parts — the MCPI React web UI and the MCPP Node.js protocol-bridge (an MCP client plus HTTP server spanning stdio, SSE, and streamable-http) — and do not mistake the proxy for a traffic-intercepting network proxy.
Expect the MCPI UI on port 6274 and the MCPP proxy on port 6277, and resolve port conflicts by overriding CLIENT_PORT and SERVER_PORT rather than changing code.

Keep the Inspector proxy bound to localhost (its default) because it can spawn local processes and reach any MCP server; bind to all interfaces with HOST=0.0.0.0 only inside a trusted, isolated network, and never expose the proxy to untrusted networks.
Reach for the MCP Inspector first: use it as an interactive, transport-agnostic way to invoke a server's tools, prompts, and resources and watch its notification stream before deeper debugging.

Rely on the proxy's default Bearer-token authentication — supplying the token non-interactively via MCP_PROXY_AUTH_TOKEN when automating — and never disable it with DANGEROUSLY_OMIT_AUTH, which enables browser-driven remote compromise (CVE-2025-49596).
Depend on the Inspector's Origin-header validation to block DNS-rebinding attacks, and widen access only by adding trusted origins to ALLOWED_ORIGINS rather than by disabling the check.
For SSE connections, authenticate to the target server with a bearer token sent in the Authorization header, overriding the header name when the server expects a different one.

Treat Inspector timeouts (MCP_SERVER_REQUEST_TIMEOUT default 300000 ms; MCP_REQUEST_MAX_TOTAL_TIMEOUT default 60000 ms) as client-side cancels independent of server-side timeouts — whichever elapses first wins — and raise them for elicitation or long-running tools.

Drive an MCP Client entirely through `async with Client(...)`: entering the block connects and negotiates and leaving it disconnects, so never call a connect()/close() pair and never reuse a Client after its block has exited.

For multi-server or complex setups, store servers in a --config file (transport auto-detected), rely on automatic selection when there is a single server or one named 'default-server', use the Server Entry / Servers File export to generate mcp.json, and remember query params override localStorage while MCP_AUTO_OPEN_ENABLED is settable only as an env var.

When constructing tool-call requests from form inputs, omit optional fields with empty values unless the schema defines a matching explicit default, preserve explicit defaults (e.g. default: null) that match the current value, always include required fields even when empty, and defer deep parameter validation to the MCP server.

Use CLI mode for scripting, automation, CI/CD, and coding-assistant feedback loops — invoking tools, resources, and prompts via --method with --tool-arg key=value or JSON — and select remote transport and headers explicitly (SSE by default, --transport http for streamable HTTP, --header for custom headers).
After changing CLI source, rebuild before trusting watch-mode results, since watch mode reflects test-file changes but not CLI source changes without a rebuild.

Design the CLI test suite for safe parallelism: run in parallel across files but sequentially within a file, make each config file unique with crypto.randomUUID(), allocate HTTP/SSE ports dynamically, depend only on built-in MCP test servers, and do not expect coverage numbers because subprocess-run code is untrackable by Vitest.
Prefer the in-memory transport session helper (create_connected_server_and_client_session) for MCP server tests instead of starting a real server or network, which yields fast, isolated tests.
While Inspector V2 is under development, scope V1 contributions to bug fixes and MCP spec compliance rather than new features.

Follow the Inspector code style: TypeScript with proper type annotations, React functional components with hooks, ES modules (not CommonJS), async/await with try/catch error handling, Prettier formatting, and small components each focused on a single responsibility.
Navigate the codebase as a monorepo of three workspaces — client (React/Vite/TypeScript/Tailwind), server (Express/TypeScript), and cli — placing changes in the workspace that owns the concern.

On Streamable HTTP, do not rely on stderr — the client will not capture it; surface diagnostics through log-message notifications, server-side log aggregation, or HTTP tooling that inspects requests, Mcp-Session-Id headers, and SSE streams.

Make logging load-bearing and structured: instrument initialization, resource access, tool execution, errors, and performance; use consistent formats, context, timestamps, and request IDs; log stack traces and track error patterns, recovery, timing, resource usage, message sizes, and latency.

Treat debug logging and debugging access as a security surface: sanitize logs, protect credentials, mask personal information, and enforce access control (verify permissions, check authentication, monitor access patterns).
Always use absolute paths in server configuration, .env files, and the command executable, because a client-launched stdio server's working directory may be undefined (e.g. / on macOS).
Declare a server's required environment variables explicitly via the client config's env key rather than relying on stdio env inheritance, which passes only a limited, platform-dependent subset.
Triage a server that fails to initialize by class of cause — path issues, configuration errors, and environment problems — rather than guessing.

Work a connection failure as an ordered checklist (client logs, server process, standalone Inspector test, protocol-version compatibility, capability negotiation); treat a -32602 Invalid params error as a likely undeclared-capability mismatch and inspect the initialize exchange.

Read the client's logs when diagnosing: know where Claude Desktop writes MCP logs (macOS ~/Library/Logs/Claude, Windows %APPDATA%\Claude\logs) and tail them live to watch connection, configuration, and runtime errors.

Use Chrome DevTools inside Claude Desktop for client-side errors — enable it via developer_settings.json (allowDevTools: true), then use the Console for errors and the Network panel for message payloads and connection timing.
Reload after changes: restart the MCP client after a configuration or code change, and for Claude Desktop fully quit and reopen it rather than only closing the window.
Follow a two-stage development loop — Inspector-driven initial development, then integration testing in the target client — and keep using the Inspector for quick iteration.

Expose the connected client session to tests through an async-generator pytest fixture that opens create_connected_server_and_client_session(app, raise_exceptions=True) with `async with` and yields the session, so teardown is automatic and server-side exceptions propagate into the test.

Consider snapshot testing (inline-snapshot's snapshot(...)) to pin expected tool results; it eases test authoring and is promoted as best practice, but it is optional and adds the inline-snapshot dependency alongside pytest.
Configure the async backend for asynchronous MCP tests: provide an anyio_backend fixture returning "asyncio" (or "trio" when running on trio) and mark async test functions with @pytest.mark.anyio.

Exercise tools through the session: await client_session.call_tool(name, arguments) and assert on the returned CallToolResult, checking both its text content (the TextContent list) and its machine-readable structuredContent.

When a tool declares an output/structured schema, call client.listTools() before client.callTool() so the client caches and validates against the tool's schemas, and assert on the result's structuredContent.
Give every FastMCP tool a clear docstring: the SDK automatically uses the function docstring as the tool's description surfaced to clients.

Test a server by passing the server object directly to `Client(...)`: the in-memory transport gives an in-process harness with no subprocess, port, or HTTP, and is the connection path the examples and tests rely on.

Read connection facts from the four read-only properties populated on entering the block — server_info, server_capabilities, protocol_version, instructions — and treat a `None` capability as 'server lacks it' and `None` instructions as 'unset'.
Use the high-level Client methods for protocol work and reach for `client.session` (the low-level ClientSession) only as an escape hatch when a needed operation is not exposed higher up.
Rely on the server deriving each tool's `input_schema` (JSON Schema) from the function's type hints, and read the full definition — name, title, description, input_schema — from `list_tools().tools`.

When presenting a tool, resource, resource template, or prompt to a human, show its title if set and fall back to its name, using `get_display_name` from `mcp.shared.metadata_utils` instead of hand-rolling the fallback.

Narrow a content or resource block with `isinstance` to its concrete type before reading its payload (`.text`, `.data`, or `.blob`); the block union is deliberate and the type checker rejects reading `.text` off an un-narrowed block.
Expect `is_error=True` for server-side failures you did not raise — for example calling a tool the server does not have — so do not assume a returned result means the tool actually ran.

List concrete resources with `list_resources()` and parameterised ones with `list_resource_templates()` (two lists because a template is not readable until filled in), and read either kind with `read_resource(uri)` passing a plain string URI that the server matches to its template.

Do not rely on `subscribe_resource`/`unsubscribe_resource` for resource-change notification on a 2026-07-28 server (those verbs are gone and return `-32601`); use the 2026 `subscriptions/listen` stream, gated on `server_capabilities.resources.subscribe`.

Discover prompts with `list_prompts()` (name, title, required arguments), render one with `get_prompt(name, arguments)` passing a string-to-string arguments dict (prompt arguments are always strings), and hand the returned `messages` (role + content block) straight to the model.

Offer argument autocompletion with `client.complete(ref, argument)` — `ref` a PromptReference or ResourceTemplateReference and `argument` a `{name, value}` of the argument and what the user has typed — and read the suggestions from `result.completion.values`.

Page every `list_*` call with a cursor loop: pass `cursor=`, collect the results, and stop when `next_cursor` is `None`; this loop is correct against every server even though `MCPServer` returns a single page.

Never assume a list call returns every item: listTools, listPrompts, listResources and listResourceTemplates are cursor-paginated, so loop passing the previous response's nextCursor as cursor until nextCursor is undefined.
In tests, construct the client as `Client(mcp, raise_exceptions=True)` to surface server-side exceptions; the flag takes effect only on in-memory connections.
Use the SDK's built-in ping() for peer health checks rather than a custom heartbeat: both client and server expose it and the remote responds automatically with no registered handler.

For a bounded health check set a millisecond timeout on client.ping(); remember the low-level server.server.ping() has no timeout option, so enforce your own deadline when pinging from the server side.

Wire progress reporting end-to-end for long-running requests: provide an onprogress callback on the client (the SDK auto-assigns the progressToken) and have the server emit notifications/progress via extra.sendNotification with the progressToken in params.
Guard server-side progress emission: send a progress notification only when extra._meta.progressToken is defined, i.e. only when the caller actually requested progress.

Make long-running calls cancellable: the client passes an AbortSignal ({ signal: controller.signal }) and calls controller.abort() to cancel; the SDK then sends notifications/cancelled and aborts the server handler through its signal.
In a cancellable server handler, poll extra.signal.aborted inside long loops/operations and stop work promptly (returning an error result) once cancellation is signalled.

Declare every capability you will use at initialize (client capabilities in the Client constructor; server capabilities inferred by McpServer from registered handlers, or declared on the low-level Server) — the SDK throws when code uses an undeclared capability.
Before using an optional server feature, inspect getServerCapabilities() after connecting and branch on what the server actually supports instead of assuming it.

Rely on the SDK's automatic protocol-version negotiation (client sends LATEST_PROTOCOL_VERSION, server returns the highest mutually supported version from SUPPORTED_PROTOCOL_VERSIONS) but handle the error the client throws when the server's version is unsupported.
Define tool input/output schemas as JSON Schema 2020-12: let McpServer with Zod convert them automatically, or supply JSON Schema directly when using the low-level Server.
Register tool and prompt input schemas with a Standard-Schema library (e.g. Zod v4) when defining the server under test.

Declare an outputSchema on tools that return structured data so the SDK validates the output, and swap in CfWorkerJsonSchemaValidator in place of the default Ajv validator when running on Cloudflare Workers.
Default to InMemoryTransport.createLinkedPair() when unit- or integration-testing MCP server logic, and reserve stdio or Streamable-HTTP transports for end-to-end transport-level tests.
Use InMemoryTransport only for test/development in-process wiring; for production in-process connections use StreamableHTTPClientTransport against a local server URL.

Establish the in-memory connection by running both client.connect() and server.connect() concurrently (e.g. await Promise.all([...])); never connect only one side or await the two connects sequentially, which deadlocks the initialize handshake.
Do not rely on a particular client-vs-server connect() ordering: pre-start messages are queued and flushed on start(), so either side may connect first.
Tear down an in-memory linked pair with a single transport.close(); it closes both ends and fires onclose, so per-transport close is unnecessary.
To test authenticated or authInfo-dependent server handlers in-process, pass authInfo through the optional option on InMemoryTransport.send().
Treat the in-memory recipe as test-runner-agnostic — it is identical under Vitest and Jest, so only the imported test primitives change between frameworks.

Select the validation profile by intent: security_focused for audits and compliance, comprehensive for thorough pre-release testing, basic for quick dev/CI checks, and development for local debugging with continue-on-failure.

Treat `protocol` as the mandatory foundation validator and respect validator dependency order (capabilities, ping, errors, security all depend on it); extend validation through the plugin model instead of ad-hoc checks.

Configure validation reproducibly through named profiles, a .mcp-validation.json config file, or the MCP_VALIDATION_CONFIG / MCP_VALIDATION_PROFILE environment variables (and tune validator parameters there) instead of ad-hoc one-off flags.

Choose the transport explicitly and supply its required endpoint and authentication: stdio is the default; HTTP needs --endpoint plus OAuth 2.0 (automatic Dynamic Client Registration, pre-registered credentials, or a personal access token); SSE needs --endpoint plus a Bearer token.
Never expose secrets in validation artifacts: rely on the tool's masking of sensitive environment-variable values and use --debug for diagnosis rather than printing raw credentials.
Give slow or parameterized servers what they need to validate: raise --timeout when startup or responses are slow, and pass server configuration through the repeatable --env flag.

Beyond the CLI, validate containerized servers through the container runtime (e.g. podman/docker) and embed validation programmatically via the API (validate_server / validate_mcp_server_command) when automating.
Standardize the container-based validation invocation: run the tool via `uv run`, use podman with `-i --rm <image>:<version>`, and append the server's package_arguments after the image name.

Treat validation warnings as non-fatal but actionable: a server can pass with warnings, so triage recurring warning categories (container images not based on UBI, mcp-scan 'NoneType' failures, and JSON-RPC error-compliance issues) instead of ignoring them.

Diagnose common validation failures as a missing required package argument or an incorrect container image reference, and recognize that servers lacking a containerized distribution cannot be validated by the container-based flow.

Validate registry servers hermetically: pass each declared environment variable with --env but use safe placeholder test values (test-user, test-password/test-secret/test-api-key, test-token, localhost with standard DB ports, and test.apps.dynatrace.com-style URLs) so no real service is contacted; infer a default only when the registry provides none.

Do not set non-stdio transport environment variables (TRANSPORT_HOST/PORT or HOST/PORT) for stdio-based servers unless the server explicitly requires a non-stdio transport, since most containerized MCP servers communicate over stdio.

When generating registry entries, extract environment-variable names verbatim from the server README (for example from `-e VARIABLE_NAME` Docker examples); never assume, invent, or standardize variable names.

Build the registry entry deterministically from the repository: clone it, derive metadata (uuid id, README-based description, GitHub repository fields), set version from the container image tag with is_latest true, model packages as a single docker entry, and store the result in registry.json conforming to the MCP registry OpenAPI schema.
Represent uncertainty by omission in registry metadata: omit is_required, default, and choices when their values are not documented, and mark usernames and sensitive values as is_secret.
Handle the no-container case explicitly: when a server has no container image, set version_detail.version to 'N/A' and leave the packages definition empty rather than fabricating package data.
